Program/Department: 2 degree programs deleted by IHL vote (BS Athletic Training, Executive MBA Gaming and Hospitality)
Notes: Mississippi IHL Board of Trustees approved deletion of two Delta State programs at its regular meeting in Jackson on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026: Bachelor of Science in Athletic Training; Executive Master of Business Administration in Gaming and Hospitality Management. Part of 15 deletions system-wide following the 2026 Academic Program Productivity Review, which covered 881 programs. Review flags programs with fewer than 18 graduates over three years (bachelor's), fewer than 12 (master's) or fewer than five (specialist and doctoral). No effective date reported. Follows Delta State's 2024 round of IHL-approved program cuts.

Program/Department: BA in Biology deleted by IHL vote
Notes: Mississippi IHL Board of Trustees approved deletion of MUW's Bachelor of Arts in Biology on Nov. 19, 2026. Part of 15 deletions system-wide following the 2026 Academic Program Productivity Review (881 programs reviewed; bachelor's threshold: under 18 graduates in three years). No effective date reported. CIP 26.0101 (Biology/Biological Sciences, General) is inferred from the program title, not stated in the article.

Program/Department: 4 graduate programs deleted by IHL vote (MA Economics, MS Technology, PhD Elementary Ed, PhD Secondary Ed)
Notes: Mississippi IHL Board of Trustees approved deletion of four Mississippi State programs on Nov. 19, 2026: Master of Arts in Economics; Master of Science in Technology; Doctor of Philosophy in Elementary Education; Doctor of Philosophy in Secondary Education. Part of 15 deletions system-wide following the 2026 Academic Program Productivity Review (881 programs reviewed; thresholds: under 18 graduates in three years for bachelor's, under 12 for master's, under five for specialist and doctoral). No effective date reported. Separately suspended, not deleted: MS in Biomedical Engineering and MS in Computational Engineering, set for deletion in October 2029 unless the university requests otherwise (conditional, not counted here). Same meeting approved new BS/BAS in Health Informatics and a Master of Health Administration at the Meridian campus (proposed start August 2027).

Program/Department: 3 programs deleted by IHL vote (PhD Preventive Medicine, certificates in Molecular Diagnostics and Radiation Therapy Technology)
Notes: Mississippi IHL Board of Trustees approved deletion of three UMMC programs on Nov. 19, 2026: Doctor of Philosophy in Preventive Medicine; Certificate Program in Molecular Diagnostics; Certificate Program in Radiation Therapy Technology. Part of 15 deletions system-wide following the 2026 Academic Program Productivity Review (881 programs reviewed; doctoral threshold: under five graduates in three years). No effective date reported.

Program/Department: 2 bachelor's programs deleted by IHL vote (BE Engineering, BA Religious Studies)
Notes: Mississippi IHL Board of Trustees approved deletion of two University of Mississippi programs on Nov. 19, 2026: Bachelor of Engineering in Engineering; Bachelor of Arts in Religious Studies. Part of 15 deletions system-wide following the 2026 Academic Program Productivity Review (881 programs reviewed; bachelor's threshold: under 18 graduates in three years). No effective date reported. Separately suspended, not deleted: PhD in Social Welfare, set for deletion in October 2029 unless the university requests otherwise (conditional, not counted here).

Program/Department: 2 degree programs deleted by IHL vote (BS Biotechnology, EdS Reading)
Notes: Mississippi IHL Board of Trustees approved deletion of two Jackson State programs on Nov. 19, 2026: Bachelor of Science in Biotechnology; Educational Specialist in Reading. Part of 15 deletions system-wide following the 2026 Academic Program Productivity Review (881 programs reviewed; thresholds: under 18 graduates in three years for bachelor's, under 12 for master's, under five for specialist and doctoral). No effective date reported. Separately suspended, not deleted: Master of Arts in Sociology, set for deletion in October 2029 unless the university requests otherwise (conditional, not counted here). Same meeting approved a new Doctor of Audiology at JSU (proposed start August 2028).

Program/Department: BA in Art deleted by IHL vote
Notes: Mississippi IHL Board of Trustees approved deletion of MVSU's Bachelor of Arts in Art on Nov. 19, 2026. Part of 15 deletions system-wide following the 2026 Academic Program Productivity Review (881 programs reviewed; bachelor's threshold: under 18 graduates in three years). No effective date reported. CIP 50.0701 (Art/Art Studies, General) is inferred from the program title, not stated in the article.

Program/Department: All 67 main-campus custodians laid off as custodial work is outsourced to HES Facilities Management
Notes: SLU is laying off all 67 main-campus custodians, who had been doing extra work to offset 35 vacancies, and outsourcing custodial services to HES Facilities Management, with a 60-day termination notice. Custodians have the option to continue employment through HES at lower pay: SEIU Local 1 says hourly wages fall $1-$1.50, a scheduled 65-cent December raise is lost, employees will pay a monthly insurance premium, and tuition benefits end except for retirement-eligible staff. SLU: "one service provider across all campuses will help keep positions filled." SLU says the union agreed to an enhanced transition package. Exact notice date not stated; date shown is the STLPR publication date.

Program/Department: 3 staff positions eliminated (Arts and Sciences admin assistant and director of academic affairs, plus a university IT position)
Notes: Three staff positions were eliminated: the administrative assistant and the director of academic affairs in the School of Arts and Sciences, and a university IT position. Provost Shari Payne announced the director of academic affairs change Nov. 13, 2026. Sources told the Globe a fourth staff position was cut, which it could not verify. The university says the positions were eliminated rather than layoffs. Arts and Sciences Dean Becky Spritz resigned the prior Thursday (about Nov. 12) for "personal and professional reasons." Karen Dwyer, first vice president of the full-time faculty union: "It felt like some sort of assault on our school of Arts and Sciences," calling it a "cost-saving measure" and saying more cuts are likely. Follows the trustee vote eliminating 4 degree programs (Nov. 2026).

Program/Department: 13 Print Services positions eliminated as printing is largely outsourced
Notes: Princeton will eliminate 13 positions in Print Services "by December due to changing business conditions, reduced demand, and financial pressures" (spokesperson Ahmad Rizvi). Large-format and bulk printing move to outside suppliers; Package and Mail Services moves under Transportation and Parking Services; the Campus Print Center has already been folded into The Service Point. Print Services is expected to be mostly outsourced by next year. Net layoffs are expected to be lower than 13 because several employees got new roles in University Services. Part of continuing budget cuts (earlier: 9 Keller Center staff, March 2026).

Program/Department: 4 degree programs eliminated by trustee vote (theatre making, grades 4-8 education, liberal studies, MS health care admin)
Notes: Point Park University's Board of Trustees voted (the weekend before Nov. 5, 2026) to eliminate four degree programs, citing under-enrollment: BA in contemporary theatre making; bachelor's in education leading to grades 4-8 certification; BA in liberal studies; and the master's in health care administration and management. Programs are closed to new admissions; current students finish under a teach-out. Liberal studies had one student and the contemporary theatre making self-directed concentration one student; the health care administration master's had been closed to new admissions for about two years. Provost Shari Payne: "We can't sustain it with one student moving forward." No faculty/staff layoffs reported.

Program/Department: Amarillo campus closing after 50 years; courses moving online, teach-out begins Dec. 31, 2026
Notes: Wayland Baptist University announced Nov. 4, 2026 that it is sunsetting its Amarillo, Texas campus after about 50 years. Effective Nov. 4 the campus no longer enrolls new students; a teach-out plan with individual academic reviews begins Dec. 31, 2026, and instruction moves primarily online. Current students will be advised through the Lubbock campus. President Donna Hedgepath: "Students have invested their time, money, and trust in Wayland, and we take our responsibility to them seriously" and "This is part of our strategic plan." No student, faculty or staff counts reported.

Program/Department: BA in Philosophy eliminated; program ends July 2027
Notes: Wichita State University President Richard Muma and Provost Monica Lounsbery decided to eliminate the BA in Philosophy, which will cease to exist in July 2027; current majors can finish. The Kansas Board of Regents had placed the program on an action plan in 2024 for falling below the 25 junior/senior majors threshold; per department chair Patrick Bondy the three-year plan ended early in 2026 with a plan to restructure around pre-law. Bondy (via The Sunflower): "I'm not thrilled about the prospect of losing the current BA program." Primary report: The Sunflower (https://thesunflower.com/110926/news/wsu-kills-foundation-of-academics/). Announcement date approximate (Daily Nous publication date).

Program/Department: 20 majors and minors eliminated and 17 tenured faculty positions cut (about a third of faculty)
Notes: Albright's Board of Trustees approved the changes Nov. 1, 2026; faculty were told by email Nov. 3. 20 majors and minors are eliminated, including dance, painting, film & video, digital and strategic communications, public health, Holocaust studies, and women's & gender studies. 17 full-time tenured professors will be terminated by August 2027 (about a third of the faculty); an internal report expects 30-35 faculty for 2027-28. Program changes take effect in 2027-28; current students get "individual advising and degree plans." Low enrollment was called the "primary driver," along with finances and new federal accountability rules. Trustees also approved an interim faculty handbook Nov. 1; faculty say they were not consulted, and more than 100 students protested Nov. 5. Faculty appeals are due within 15 business days. Last public enrollment: 1,230 undergraduates (fall 2024).

Program/Department: 46 administrative positions eliminated via layoffs, retirements and closed vacancies
Notes: Seton Hall University officials announced in October 2026 that they eliminated 46 administrative positions as part of a cost-cutting effort unveiled earlier in 2026. The reduction came from a mix of eliminated open positions, layoffs and retirements; the vice president for finance also launched a voluntary separation program whose savings are not yet known. Reported by Inside Higher Ed (Nov. 3, 2026). Exact October announcement date not given; 2026-10-31 used as an approximation.

Program/Department: 8 Title III grant-funded staff positions eliminated (fundraising, alumni engagement)
Notes: Jackson State University notified employees in late October 2026 that eight staff jobs funded by a federal Title III grant, in areas including fundraising and alumni engagement, will be eliminated by the end of 2026. University officials said the grant funds were reallocated rather than necessarily lost, without giving details. Reported by Inside Higher Ed (Nov. 3, 2026), citing Mississippi Today (Oct. 30, 2026: https://mississippitoday.org/2026/10/30/jackson-state-layoffs-federal-funding/).

Program/Department: 18 graduate programs cut and 100+ staff positions eliminated to close $65M gap
Notes: [staff] Preliminary academic modifications proposal released Oct. 28, 2026 to address a $65M structural deficit (average unit cut 7.25%, down from 10% forecast). More than 100 staff positions eliminated, about one-third vacant; no tenure-track faculty layoffs, though 61 professors enrolled in a retirement program shrinking faculty over two years. Libraries: 5% cut, up to 8 FTE. 18 graduate programs eliminated, including Folklore, Operations and Business Analytics, and the Ph.D. in Management (admissions already paused). Recruitment paused for Ph.D. programs in Architecture; Landscape Architecture; History of Art and Architecture; and Planning, Public Policy and Management. Art MFA capped at 5 students/year. Mergers: Classics with Religious Studies; Earth Sciences with Geography; College of Design with School of Music and Dance; possibly German and Scandinavian, Romance Languages, and REEES. Savings: $17.6M administrative, $25.8M academic. Admissions stop fall 2027; master's teach-outs end spring 2028; Ph.D. closures by ~spring 2032. Final decision by President Karl Scholz expected early December 2026.

Program/Department: Institution closing after 2026-27; final day of instruction Aug. 20, 2027
Notes: Board of trustees voted unanimously on Oct. 27, 2026 to close the private Roman Catholic university in Great Falls, Mont., founded in 1932 by the Sisters of Providence. Final day of instruction is Aug. 20, 2027. The school had 630 students and 244 total employees (Daily Montanan). Reasons: continued enrollment decline and significant financial pressures; 2025 revenue $28.6M vs. expenses $35.6M; financial exigency declared in December 2025; Providence Health support of about $8M a year had been cut. Prior restructuring, expense cuts and merger/acquisition talks did not yield a viable model. Students will finish, use NWCCU-approved teach-outs with partner institutions, or transfer; Montana University System pledged help. President Caroline Goulet: "Despite those efforts, we could not find a financially sustainable way forward." Staff meetings on employment timelines began Oct. 28.

Program/Department: 14 programs on administrative hold incl. political science, Spanish, environmental studies majors and Holocaust & genocide studies MA
Notes: Keene State placed 14 programs on "administrative hold" (no new students may enroll as of Fall 2026). Majors: BA political science, BS sustainability studies, BA environmental studies, BA Spanish, BS education (early childhood development). Minors: early childhood development, political science, human resource management, campaigns and elections, medieval and early modern studies, geography, Spanish. Graduate: MA Holocaust and genocide studies; certificate in applied genocide prevention. Three (BS ed early childhood, BA Spanish, ECD minor) were already on hold last year. Reasons cited: faculty retirements, staffing, low enrollment, redundancy across NH public systems. No timeline for the holds; programs may be revised, combined or phased out. College said it is premature to speculate on layoffs. Current students can still graduate. Originally reported by the Keene Sentinel.

Program/Department: 52 programs discontinued (19 associate degrees, 13 certificates, 20 dormant legacy programs) after portfolio review
Notes: BC3 trustees unanimously approved two motions on Wednesday (likely Oct. 21, 2026). Motion 1 discontinues 32 programs (19 associate degree, 13 certificate) identified in an academic portfolio review. Motion 2 formally discontinues 20 legacy programs not offered in at least 10 years. 18 students are enrolled in five of the affected programs; teach-out plans are in place and advisers have contacted them. College says "no layoffs will occur as a result of the actions" and "Credentials earned in the discontinued programs remain valid." Practical nursing certificate remains active; new radiologic technologist cohort starts fall 2027.

Program/Department: Center for Early Childhood Education at Fort Hill (childcare center) closing June 2027
Notes: [staff] Smith announced by email Oct. 19, 2026 (VP of HR Anne-Marie Szmyt) that the Center for Early Childhood Education at Fort Hill, opened in 1926 and serving about 80 children in seven classrooms, will close June 4, 2027. Union teacher Rachel Connally says about 30 staff jobs are at risk. Smith will replace it with an expanded flexible childcare benefit for employees with children up to age 12. Smith: "nor is it a budget-relieving measure." Parents and the union (UAW Local 322, in first-contract bargaining) link the closure to unionization.

Program/Department: Staff reduction in force of just under 9%, mostly central administration
Notes: TU announced a reduction in force of just under 9% of its staff, primarily in central administration, and will leave several vacancies unfilled. University statement: "We made the difficult decision to eliminate some staff positions – primarily in central administration – and will let several vacancies go unfilled." "No faculty positions were eliminated, and students should not be affected negatively." TU declined to give a headcount. The Chronicle (citing Tulsa World) reports changes take effect Nov. 2, 2026, alongside a short-term hiring freeze.

Program/Department: 47 degree programs recommended for closure, 11 at University Park, under academic program review
Notes: Penn State's final Academic Program Portfolio Review (APPR) recommendations call for closing 47 degree programs (down from 49 in the spring preliminary list): 11 at University Park and 36 at other campuses. University Park programs include Professional Photography (BDES), Elementary and Kindergarten Education (BS), Middle Level Education (BS), World Languages Education (BS), Security and Risk Analysis (BS), Multidisciplinary Studies (BA/AA), Planetary Science and Astronomy (BS) and Geosciences (BA). 784 undergraduates (about 1.1%) are affected; 9 programs have no students. 15 programs have already filed phase-out or enrollment-suspension plans. Recommendations still need Faculty Senate review and final approval from Provost Fotis Sotiropoulos; students will be supported to finish their degrees.

Institution: Minnesota State Community and Technical College
Program/Department: Detroit Lakes campus closing by summer 2028; programs relocating starting fall 2027
Notes: M State announced Oct. 6, 2026 that its Detroit Lakes campus (111 students) will close, staying open until at least summer 2028, with phased program moves starting fall 2027. Radiologic technology moves to the Moorhead campus; nursing stays in Detroit Lakes through a planned lease with a local partner. About 40 employees are based at the campus, though many work collegewide or remotely. Closure saves about $1M a year and avoids $18M+ in capital needs. Still requires Minnesota State Board of Trustees approval; public meeting Nov. 5. Comes as the Minnesota State system warns of broader campus closures and mergers. Update (2026-11-18, MPR News): The Minnesota State Board of Trustees unanimously approved the closure on Nov. 18, 2026. The campus is expected to close in summer 2028; nursing moves to a new off-campus Detroit Lakes location and radiologic technology moves to the Moorhead campus. Source: https://www.mprnews.org/story/2026/11/18/minnesota-state-board-votes-to-close-of-detroit-lakes-campus

Program/Department: 21 positions eliminated (14 faculty, 7 staff) to address $20M structural deficit
Notes: Stockton University notified its CWA and AFT unions of plans to lay off 14 faculty and 7 staff, the university's first layoffs, effective at the end of the 2026-27 academic year. The cuts address a $20M structural deficit worsened by declining enrollment and reduced state aid. Unions rallied in Galloway in response. President Joe Bertolino: "We recognize the very real impact this decision will have on them and their families."

Program/Department: Sternberg Museum of Natural History closing Dec. 18, 2026 after $2.4M state funding cut
Notes: FHSU President Tisa Mason announced Sept. 28, 2026 that the Sternberg Museum will close to the public Dec. 18 after the Kansas Legislature cut $2.4M in recurring state funding, with another cut likely in 2028. Closing saves about $850K, the largest piece of the budget fix. The museum costs about $1.3M a year, brings in about $470K, and sits in a building with $20M+ in deferred maintenance. Museum faculty and staff stay through the academic year to review collections and keep specimens used in research and teaching. FHSU still needs about $1M in other cuts plus $550K more. Update (2026-10-28, Kansas Reflector/HPPR; Inside Higher Ed): Closure reversed. President Tisa Mason announced Oct. 26 that the Sternberg Museum will remain open after donors gave about $1.2M (FHSU Foundation drive matched up to $1M by the Bob and Pat Schmidt Foundation). Mason called it "breathing room" for one year while the university develops a sustainable business plan; the museum's budget gap is about $830,000.

Program/Department: About 175 positions eliminated (75 faculty, 100 staff) across Bloomsburg, Lock Haven and Mansfield
Notes: Commonwealth University expects to lay off up to 175 employees (about 75 faculty and 100 staff) across all three campuses to address a recurring structural deficit. Faculty notices due by Oct. 30, 2026; staff notices in January 2027; cuts effective July 1, 2027. Retirements and resignations may lower the final number. First reported by WPSU.

Program/Department: 9 academic programs terminated, including Mathematics and Mechanical Engineering Technology
Notes: Board of Trustees voted Sept. 25, 2026 to terminate 9 programs that failed SC Commission on Higher Education enrollment and graduation standards for over 10 years: Business Education, Professional Land Surveying, Art Education, Social Studies Education, Jr. High/Middle School Education, Mathematics, Technology Teacher Education (Industrial), Mechanical Engineering Technology and Dramatic Arts Education. Mechanical Engineering Technology has 82 enrolled students; four other programs have 29 combined; four have zero enrollment. Current students covered by state-mandated teach-out. Only 37% of SC State programs met state standards vs. 77% statewide.

Program/Department: About 20 faculty laid off, including tenured and 5 in History, to close $18M deficit
Notes: Bowie State, Maryland's oldest HBCU, is laying off about 20 faculty, including at least one tenured professor, to address an $18 million structural deficit. At least 5 History faculty received notices. Layoffs take effect one year after notice, so faculty teach through the 2026-27 year. Comes on top of 75 staff positions cut in spring 2026 and follows department mergers and restructuring, and after a record fundraising campaign of nearly $130M (including $50M from MacKenzie Scott). President Aminta Breaux: "Our circumstances require more than a one-year response."

Program/Department: Faculty retrenchments and staff layoffs announced to close $19M FY2028 budget gap
Notes: President Joan Ferrini-Mundy and Provost Gabriel Paquette announced September 17 in joint letter that faculty retrenchments and staff layoffs will be required to close $19M FY2028 shortfall. Additional measures: eliminate one-fifth of currently vacant positions; consolidate course sections; decrease instructional budgets; long-term caps on course sizes and program closures for low-enrollment programs. Revenue strategy: increase undergraduate retention and out-of-state/transfer/adult enrollment by 1%. Even with vacancy cuts and revenue growth, projected unaddressed deficit remains $5.7M — requiring personnel reductions. Headcount and affected positions not yet determined; budget proposal presented to trustees January 2027. UMaine historically avoided large-scale cuts despite peer institution pressures. Causes: operating costs outpacing state funding and tuition; $1B+ deferred maintenance; declining enrollment; federal funding and financial aid policy changes restricting international students; flat or declining tuition revenue. 2,400+ employees; 7,308 full-time undergrads fall 2025. Second UMaine entry — prior entry covers March 2026 Faculty Senate vote on program suspensions (also in database).

Program/Department: 14 positions eliminated — 4% of workforce — to address $6.5M two-year budget gap
Notes: [staff] 14 employees (4% of ~400-person workforce) laid off week of September 10. University Community FAQ confirms no class cancellations. Cuts address $6.5M needed over next two years. University pursuing enrollment growth and new revenue opportunities. No plans to close. Baptist-affiliated; 120+ year history; Boiling Springs NC. Interim President Nathaniel Evans leading institution. Prior action: head football coach recently terminated (separate from budget cuts). Head softball coach contract non-renewed end of last school year following internal investigation into alleged inappropriate relationships.

Program/Department: Up to 800 positions eliminated across advancement, HR, finance, IT and marketing over 12 months
Notes: [staff] Up to 800 positions eliminated over next 12 months across advancement, HR, finance, IT, and marketing — largest single workforce reduction in U of U history. University stated cuts are unrelated to recent 10% federal funding cut; described as long-planned restructuring for operational efficiency. No academic programs or faculty positions affected. Fourth U of U entry in database — separate from 32 advising layoffs (May 2026), Sandy Center campus closure (August 2026), and Utah Athletics private equity restructuring (June 2026).

Program/Department: Office of Digital Learning and Inquiry (DLINQ) eliminated as standalone unit; 8 positions affected
Notes: [staff] Middlebury College is ending its Office of Digital Learning and Inquiry (DLINQ) as a standalone unit. Eight positions are affected: five employees lose their jobs and three were offered entry-level roles at lower pay grades. Employees were told by email in September 2026 (exact date not reported; email shared with Inside Higher Ed by the college's AAUP chapter).

Program/Department: 65 Viterbi School of Engineering IT staff laid off in departmental restructure
Notes: USC filed a California WARN notice on Sept. 1, 2026 to lay off 65 employees at the Viterbi School of Engineering, mostly IT roles such as software and network engineers and web developers. A staffer said nearly the entire Viterbi IT department is affected. Layoffs take effect Nov. 4 and may continue through Dec. 3. USC cited funding cutbacks and a restructure "aligning our teams, talent, and resources with the university's long-term strategic priorities." Follows 900+ USC layoffs in 2025 amid a budget gap of $230M or more.

Program/Department: WPSU public radio/TV station employees laid off as ownership transfers to WHYY
Notes: [staff] 31 full-time WPSU employees laid off September 1: 22 staff + 9 unionized technical service employees. WHYY making job offers to many. Timeline: June 2025 — Penn State cut WPSU funding 20% ($800K) triggering 5+ layoffs, reducing staff from 82 to ~44. September 11, 2025 — Board Finance Committee rejected $17M WHYY transfer deal (no employment guarantees). September 15, 2025 — Penn State announced WPSU closure by June 30, 2026. October 2025 — Board reversed course, approved revised deal with WHYY raising $17.3M over 5 years instead. August 2026 — FCC transfer application under review; public comment period met. September 1, 2026 — all remaining 31 employees laid off pending FCC approval (~mid-September expected). WPSU-TV reaches 515,000 households; WPSU-FM serves 450,000 listeners across central/northern Pennsylvania. 60-year station. Federal public media funding cuts (Congress canceled CPB funding) plus Penn State budget pressures ($3.4M annual institutional subsidy unsustainable) drove closure decision. Third Penn State entry in database — separate from Commonwealth Campus closures and 49 program cuts entries.

Program/Department: 180 positions eliminated across academic, administrative and operational areas — second consecutive year of layoffs
Notes: 180 positions eliminated across academic, administrative and operational functions — university cited "changes in workflows, enrollment trends and technology" shifting priorities. No degree programs eliminated. Employees receiving HR support. Second consecutive year of major layoffs: prior round May 2025 cut 120 employees (5% of workforce) also citing "long-term sustainability." Founder Jon Phelps reportedly shifting investment interest toward Craftmasters, a new traditional trades school chain. Dream Lofts dorm project (570 beds, $Xm) still proceeding on University Blvd — expected 2028 debut. Private for-profit institution in Winter Park FL; entertainment, media, arts and technology focus. ~6,700 employees pre-cuts.

Program/Department: Staff layoffs approved by trustees amid soaring health-benefit and utility costs
Notes: Brookdale's Board of Trustees approved staff reductions on Aug. 25, 2026; President David M. Stout confirmed the layoffs Aug. 26 in an email to the Asbury Park Press. Number of positions not released (local legislators said "dozens of employees"). Reasons: health benefit costs rising from $11M (2025) to a projected $24.3M next fiscal year, utility bills up nearly 90% since FY2020, enrollment about 6% below pre-pandemic. Stout: "the cost of operating the College has increased substantially faster than enrollment." Two River Times (Oct. 2026) also reported the layoffs.

Program/Department: Additional staff layoffs (at least 14 union staff) amid continued cost-cutting
Notes: Staff were notified Aug. 20-21, 2026 that their positions were eliminated; the United Staff of Columbia College confirmed 14 of its members were laid off. The college did not disclose the total number of positions or areas affected; vacant positions will not be filled. Office of the President email: "As a part of our continued work to align Columbia's operating structure with our current enrollment and fiscal realities, we have made additional staff reductions." Latest in a series of cuts since 2024 tied to a ~$40M deficit. faculty_affected = 14 is a minimum (union members only).

Program/Department: Sandy Center satellite campus closing January 1, 2027 — state-mandated budget changes cited
Notes: Sandy Center satellite campus (10011 Centennial Pkwy, Sandy UT) closing effective January 1, 2027. U has had Sandy presence 25+ years; moved to current larger facility 2015. 660 students enrolled in Sandy Center classes fall 2026; only 33 register exclusively at Sandy (rest also take online or main campus classes). Fall 2026 classes continue as planned. Spring 2027 and beyond: students directed to online and main campus options. Continuing Education, youth programming, and Osher Lifelong Learning Institute offerings continue at other U locations. Salt Lake Tribune reports closure driven by state-mandated budget changes (HB 265). No programs eliminated — courses continue at other locations. Staff positions affected but headcount not disclosed.

Program/Department: 101 courses removed from core curriculum — 40% reduction under Texas SB 37
Notes: UH System Board of Regents approved August 20 removal of 101 courses from core curriculum — 40% of approximately 260 current core offerings — under Texas Senate Bill 37 (2025) compliance. Courses removed from core (still available as electives): Introduction to Women's Studies, Introduction to LGBT Studies, Introduction to Ethnic Studies, Black Liberation Theology, Mexican American Urban Communities, Latino Leadership/Activism/Organizing, Intro to Global Climate Change, Sexuality and Society, Black Liberation Studies, American Literature to 1865, Applied Technical Statistics, Technology Entrepreneurship, Liberals vs. Conservatives: FDR to Present, and ~87 others spanning humanities, social sciences, and sciences. 700 students enroll each semester in LGBT Studies alone. Core curriculum now keeps ~160 courses. Faculty senate dissolved under SB 37 — stripped of curriculum decision-making power given to Board of Regents. AAUP chapter urged pause citing lack of transparency and rushed process. Some faculty said review encouraged self-censorship via "academic commitment" to critical thinking over indoctrination. Courses removed lose core status but not catalog status — fewer students will take them, threatening enrollment in small departments. SB 37 also required UNT ($45M deficit, also in database), Texas A&M (WGST closure, in database), Texas Tech, and UT Austin to review core curricula. UH already has prior entry for Religious Studies BA closure (May 22, 2026, in database). Regents must recertify core curriculum every 5 years under SB 37.

Program/Department: 21 staff laid off and 27 vacant positions frozen — president and administrators took pay cuts
Notes: [staff] 21 staff positions eliminated + 27 vacant positions frozen following spring analysis. President Jody Fournier and other administrators also took pay cuts alongside layoffs. Cuts driven by declining enrollment and revenues. Fournier: cuts "necessary to balance staffing levels." Private liberal arts university; Baldwin City KS; United Methodist-affiliated; ~900 students.

Program/Department: Center for Intercultural Engagement closed and positions eliminated — $8.9M reallocation under HB 265
Notes: Center for Intercultural Engagement (CIE) permanently closed under Utah HB 265 compliance and DEI prohibition law. Less than 2% of ~2,300 full-time employees laid off (fewer than 46 total). Nearly one-third of eliminated positions were vacant, retiring, or contract-expired. Surviving employees receive severance and benefits through end of June. HB 265 requires UVU to reallocate $8.9M from 2025-26 budget toward highest-value programs. CIE closure driven by combination of budget pressure and state law prohibiting DEI-labeled programs. Academic and administrative positions affected across multiple departments. Town hall held August 19 to update employees. Strategic reinvestment plan being developed as directed by HB 265. Utah's largest public university by enrollment (~43,000 students).

Program/Department: Program of African Studies loses research center status — 2 staff positions cut
Notes: Program of African Studies (founded 1948) moved from Office of Research to Office of the Provost — loses status as a research center, retaining only academic/teaching functions. 2 staff positions eliminated in transition. Faculty continue to teach classes and conduct research; undergraduate and graduate degrees in African studies continue unaffected. Officials said move will "re-energize" program and "ensure its success going forward." No financial figures disclosed. Evanston IL; private research university.

Program/Department: Master's in Industrial and Organizational Psychology eliminated
Notes: Nebraska Board of Regents voted unanimously August 14 to eliminate UNO MS in Industrial and Organizational Psychology. Cited low enrollment. Part of 9-program elimination across NU system in same August 14 board vote. Student regent Aditi Rai: "It is not sustainable to keep increasing tuition. It is not sustainable to keep making cuts." Regent Jim Scheer: "It's reached a point where we try to reduce and cut things but the last time I knew, you can't cut a bone with a knife."

Program/Department: BA and BS in Ethnic Studies and BS in Insect Science eliminated — third round of NU cuts
Notes: Nebraska Board of Regents voted unanimously August 14 to eliminate 3 UNL programs: BA in Ethnic Studies, BS in Ethnic Studies, BS in Insect Science. Former UNL professor Ellen Moore spoke in opposition: "Removing Ethnic Studies as a major because of an arbitrary baseline number of majors, strips away a meaningful opportunity that connects scholarship across disciplines." Decision cited low enrollment, accreditation concerns, and faculty retirements. Board simultaneously approved 4.25% annual budget increase request for 2027-29 cycle pending state legislature approval. Part of ongoing NU system-wide cuts — third major round at UNL after December 2025 department closures (4 departments, 541 students, 51 positions) and Gender and Sexuality Center closure (June 2026) — both in database.

Program/Department: Post-baccalaureate in Infectious Disease Epidemiology eliminated
Notes: Nebraska Board of Regents voted unanimously August 14 to eliminate UNMC post-baccalaureate certificate in Infectious Disease Epidemiology. Cited low enrollment. Medical student Alexander Belaschenko raised concerns about future of rural and underserved community medical care: "I don't think that the future of this university's financial security can rely on a model where students need to take out additional high interest private loans." Part of 9-program elimination across NU system in same August 14 board vote.

Program/Department: Early Care and Education program closed — Krieger and University Village childcare centers shutting June 2027
Notes: Provost Darnell Hunt notified parents August 13 that Krieger Center and University Village Early Care and Education centers will close June 30, 2027 — program deemed "not sustainable." Centers serve UCLA students, faculty, and staff children ages 2 months to 6 years; infant tuition ~$3,300/month for UCLA affiliates. Closure driven by UCLA $220M budget deficit. Prior actions at ECE this year: Fernald Center closed March 2025 (students moved to Krieger); food/formula program cut April 2026 then reversed after parent protests; tuition raised 4% for 2026-27. Teacher Christopher Rodriguez convicted April 2025 on 9 counts including child sexual abuse (employed at both Fernald and Krieger centers). About 60 parents protested outside Murphy Hall August 18. UCLA FAQ states transition assistance available from mid-September; cannot guarantee placement elsewhere. International doctoral students and researchers disproportionately affected — no family networks in LA. Part of broader national trend: Purdue, Shawnee State, UNO, University of Louisville all closing on-campus childcare amid rising costs. Separate from 27 DTS staff layoffs (July 2026) also in database.

Program/Department: 60 positions affected — 17 laid off, 8 early retirements, 35 vacant positions eliminated or frozen
Notes: 60 total positions impacted: 17 layoffs/retrenchments (affected employees notified week of August 24); 8 early separation retirement packages accepted (positions end December 31, 2026); 15 vacant positions eliminated; 20 vacant/expected-vacant positions placed on hold. Additional cuts: 21 graduate assistant positions reduced; lease for Hubbard Building space ended; professional development funding for administrators frozen; institutional equipment purchases reduced; credit card transaction fees shifted to students (~$1.4M annually). Compensation = 75% of general fund budget — personnel cuts unavoidable per President Edward Inch. Deficit driven by rising operating costs, limited state support, structural funding challenges. Enrollment remains strong but insufficient to close gap. Affected bargaining units: faculty (IFO), administrative and service staff (MSUAASF), AFSCME, MAPE. Revenue growth strategy: expand graduate/professional education, grow online/hybrid offerings, increase adult learner outreach, strengthen employer partnerships, expand select athletics rosters, increase scholarship fundraising. Broader reorganization effort to follow in coming months. Part of Minnesota higher ed funding pressure alongside University of Minnesota (230 jobs, June 2026, also in database).

Program/Department: 160 faculty and staff eliminated — financial exigency declared as international enrollment collapses
Notes: Illinois Tech declared state of "extraordinary financial exigency" July 29 and issued layoff notices to ~160 faculty and staff effective August 11. Up to one-third of faculty terminated — tenured faculty fired with 2 weeks notice and 6 weeks severance. Chicago-Kent Law School (Downtown Loop campus) also affected — approximately one-fifth of law faculty. Layoffs disproportionately affected women faculty per Brian Leiter. Root cause: international enrollment collapsed — lost ~1,200 international graduate students between fall 2024 and 2025 (40%+ of students from outside US; 60% of graduate students). Faculty senate voted no confidence in President Raj Echambadi and Provost Elizabeth Hudson July 28 — day before notices. Board of Trustees reaffirmed confidence in leadership. 3 interdisciplinary colleges to replace 7 separate colleges in restructuring: Tech Futures, Design Futures, Professional Futures. 7,500 total students enrolled fall 2025; 14:1 student-faculty ratio maintained post-cuts. Main campus in Bronzeville; Chicago-Kent law center in Loop. Community concern: Illinois Tech is Bronzeville's major institutional employer and anchor. Federal research cutbacks and demographic decline cited alongside international enrollment restrictions as contributing factors.

Program/Department: Permanent institution closure — academic operations suspended indefinitely after August 2026
Notes: Board announced July 29 suspension of academic operations indefinitely following summer semester ending August 2026. Board: "could not continue academic operations responsibly" after "extensive efforts to address financial challenges, pursue strategic partnerships, and identify sustainable paths forward." No plans to resume operations. Only essential staff retained to support students, preserve records, oversee assets. Three teach-out partners: Messiah University (PA), Eastern University (PA), Southeastern University (FL) — all Christian colleges. 589 students enrolled fall 2024 (~one-third smaller than a decade prior). Founded 1939 as Bible institute; Assemblies of God affiliated. June 25, 2026: Middle States Commission on Higher Education issued show-cause order requiring UVF to prove financial sustainability — accreditation loss risk triggered final decision. MSCHE had been pressing for financial disclosures for years; last audited statement dates to fiscal 2021 showing steep tuition revenue declines. $30.8M debt in FY2021; total property $25.6M including long-unsold conference center. 2019: Virginia campus closed. Board: "Until the very last moment, we had significant reason to believe there was a sustainable path forward." Part of wave of small Christian college closures 2025-26: Anna Maria, Lourdes, Providence Christian, Trinity Christian, Hampshire — all in database.

Program/Department: 502 incoming students unenrolled days before fall 2026 move-in over payment deadlines
Notes: 502 incoming students unenrolled July 24 — days before fall 2026 move-in — after Howard determined they had not met payment, payment plan or financial aid requirements by university deadlines. Students and families said they believed financial aid was still being processed. Howard acknowledged it had not previously enforced deadlines this strictly. Partial reversal: 46 students reinstated as of July 27; additional appeals under review. SUNY and CUNY offering guaranteed admission to New York residents affected; campuses include Albany, Binghamton, Buffalo, Buffalo State, New Paltz, Oneonta and Stony Brook. University of the District of Columbia extended enrollment deadline to August 7. New York offering $800 credit to offset nonrefundable Howard enrollment deposits. Interim President Wayne Frederick defended decision on CNN July 26. HBCU; Washington DC flagship; ~10,500 students.

Program/Department: FAS Wave 5 — 36 College staff laid off, 28 offered role change or layoff
Notes: [staff] Wave 5 of FAS restructuring July 24: 36 employees directly laid off + 28 offered choice between changed role and layoff = 64 positions in scope. High-profile departures: Writing Center Director Jane Rosenzweig, Harvard Writing Project Director James Herron, Dean of Student Services Mike Burke (26 years at Harvard). Office of Student Services dismantled. Phillips Brooks House hardest hit: 10 of 23 in-scope employees affected. Employees informed via Zoom calls Thursday July 24. Some may be hired into new cluster roles — final net layoff count pending. FAS Dean Hoekstra and Dean of Administration Petrofsky confirmed more waves coming. McKinsey-developed cluster restructuring model. Part of $365M FAS structural deficit closure. Prior Harvard entries in database: Radcliffe (April), FAS senior leaders (June), Wave 4 July 14.

Program/Department: 40 employees laid off — first confirmed round toward $60M in cuts to address $85M deficit
Notes: 40 employees laid off July 8 across multiple schools and administrative units — specific areas not disclosed. Separate from 77 faculty who took voluntary retirement incentive departing end of June 2026 saving $15M annually. Running total: 77 voluntary retirements + 40 layoffs = 117 positions eliminated so far. Additional layoffs expected — President Fry said in June "some reduction in force is inevitable" since ~70% of budget is compensation/benefits. Faculty union TAUP demanding transparency and participation in decision-making. Vacant position eliminations also ongoing. Part of $60M total cuts needed to address $85M projected FY2027 deficit on $1.3B operating budget. Target: balanced budget over next three years. Enrollment decline and federal funding uncertainty are root causes. Largest public research university in Pennsylvania; ~34,000 students. Fall 2026 enrollment deposits trending up vs prior year.

Program/Department: 250+ fewer employees for 2026-27 through non-renewals, attrition and phased retirements
Notes: NAU began the 2026-27 academic year with more than 250 fewer employees than the prior year. The cuts came through non-renewals, attrition, and voluntary and phased retirements; NAU did not say how many were layoffs or which positions were affected. Projected fall 2026 enrollment is down 2,854 FTE students; FY2027 revenue is projected down about 6% and expenses down about 8%. Officials said NAU is "aligning the size of the university to the students we serve." A CollegeCuts tip (Oct 2026) reports about 70 faculty laid off plus incentivized early retirements; not independently confirmed.

Program/Department: 25 positions eliminated including CFO and VP-level admins to redirect $3.7M to faculty and research
Notes: [staff] 25 employees terminated week of July 2: CFO Tommy Smith ($390K/year, 1-year tenure; duties moving to LSU System CFO Brandi Roberts); VP of Engagement/Civil Rights/Title IX Todd Manuel ($329K/year; hired 2022 by former President Tate); 16 marketing/communications staff (writers, video producers, photographers); 7 additional Office of Engagement positions (director of institutional engagement, director of learning and development, others). Saves ~$3.7M annually redirected to faculty hiring and research funding. Goal: become top-50 research university (currently ranked 83rd per NSF 2024). Part of broader LSU restructuring: Board split previously combined president/chancellor role into two — President Rousse (public-facing) and Chancellor Dalton (academics/research). All LSU research campuses (main campus, AgCenter, Pennington Biomedical, medical schools in New Orleans and Shreveport) being unified under single research enterprise. Future marketing handled by CCO Meg Casper Sunstrom and yet-to-be-determined team. No academic programs affected.

Program/Department: 80 vacant positions eliminated and filled faculty and staff cuts announced — FY2027 raises suspended
Notes: 80 vacant positions eliminated (35 open faculty + 45 open staff) plus unspecified cuts to filled faculty and staff positions. FY2027 merit salary increases suspended entirely. President Edward Feser announced July 1. Enrollment fell more than 2,000 students (15%) YoY — 13,307 undergraduate/post-baccalaureate students for year ending May 2026. S&P Global revised bond outlook to "negative" June 23 citing inability to maintain enrollment and revenue. Third consecutive round of SLU cuts: Round 1 (October 2024) — 23 layoffs + 130 vacancies frozen under Pestello; Round 2 — balanced budget FY2025 (no major new layoffs); Round 3 (this action). Feser: "Revenue realities mean the university will need to operate with fewer people and resources." Strategic plan draft forthcoming. Filled position cuts not quantified publicly — total impact higher than 80. Separate from April 2026 tennis program cuts also in database.

Program/Department: 27 digital and technology services staff laid off amid $220M deficit — union alleges contract violation
Notes: [staff] 27 employees in Digital and Technology Services (DTS) department laid off late June as part of larger technology reorganization. UCLA faces $220M projected deficit for 2025-26 fiscal year. UPTE-CWA 9119 union alleging contract violation — union contract requires alternative process before layoffs including offering open positions to qualified employees; union demanding UCLA rescind layoffs. "We call on UCLA to quickly rescind these layoffs. Thousands of IT employees recently joined our tech union because our contract requires alternatives to layoffs, providing them the security to do their best work" — Max Belasco, UPTE-CWA 9119 co-chair. Savings from layoffs not disclosed. Part of broader UC system financial pressure; UCLA deficit among largest in UC system.

Program/Department: 43 academic majors and minors eliminated — replaced by dozens of workforce-focused certificates
Notes: 43 academic majors and minors eliminated as part of academic redesign at Pennsylvania Western University (formed from merger of Edinboro, California, and Clarion universities of Pennsylvania in 2022). Simultaneously adding dozens of new workforce-focused certificates. PennWest California campus arts programs specifically named in article headline. Part of broader restructuring of the system created by the 2022 merger of three PASSHE universities. Specific program names not available from metadata alone — article paywalled. PASSHE system facing enrollment and funding pressures across all campuses.

Program/Department: 230 jobs eliminated through layoffs and attrition to close $44M structural deficit
Notes: 230 jobs cut (some through layoffs, others through attrition) as part of $5.4B system operating budget approved 9-1 by Board of Regents June 27. 3.8% tuition increase for most students — 6th consecutive year of tuition hikes. $44M structural deficit addressed through combination of job cuts, tuition increase, and unit-level reductions. College of Liberal Arts already running $12M deficit; 25 of 31 liberal arts departments reported reducing course offerings in spring 2026 survey. Teaching assistant budget cut 20% in fall — TAs supervising more sections. Faculty given 3% raise; adjunct professor budget increased $5M. Prior year (FY2026): 6.5% tuition increase + $98M in academic program cuts (7% reduction). AAUP Twin Cities chapter strongly opposed: "second year of unprecedented cuts." President Rebecca Cunningham: budget "addresses challenges the best we can." Regent Tadd Johnson: "Nobody likes it but we have to move forward." Regent Robyn Gulley sole dissenting vote. Separately: 200 additional jobs at risk from federal funding cuts (AFSCME reported) — not included in the 230 count.

Program/Department: 110 administrative staff laid off as federal research portfolio continues to shrink
Notes: 110 employees primarily in administrative functions laid off across Bloomberg School of Public Health, Carey Business School, and central administration. "As our federal research portfolio shrinks the infrastructure around it must change in parallel" — spokesperson Doug Donovan. Prior cost-management: hiring freeze, pausing raises for employees earning $80K+, reducing discretionary spending, eliminating vacant positions, 20% reduction in 5-year capital project spending — all proved insufficient. JHU simultaneously increasing in-house research awards by $50M and nearly doubled lobbying spending since 2024. Hiring freeze continues. Second distinct layoff round — separate from March 2025 USAID-driven 2,200 cuts also in database. Trump administration terminated $6.9B-$8.2B in university grants nationally per Center for American Progress.

Program/Department: Downtown Library, LibTech lending desk and Curriculum Materials Center closed with no notice
Notes: [staff] Three library units closed simultaneously June 25 with zero advance notice: Addition Financial Downtown Campus Library (served 20+ downtown-exclusive majors including Legal Studies and Health Informatics); LibTech desk at John C. Hitt Library (laptops, DSLR cameras, tablets, microphones, lighting kits, calculators — free equipment loans for students); Curriculum Materials Center on main campus (PreK-12 materials for education majors and local teachers). Staff informed by HR in person or by phone day-of — some mid-shift; told not to return. UCF HR explicitly planned to give no advance warning to "limit the upset." UCF cited "comprehensive review of library usage, academic priorities, and available resources." Actual reason per Florida Rep. Anna Eskamani: UCF did not receive expected preeminence status funding from Tallahassee ($10M+ annually for faculty raises and services). Prior closure: Universal Orlando Foundation Library at Rosen College of Hospitality Management permanently closed April 25, 2025. Student workers also terminated without notice. Main campus John C. Hitt Library and downtown tech lending desk remain open. Students directed to UCF Libraries feedback form and Board of Trustees meetings. 73,000+ student enrollment — one of the largest universities in the US.

Program/Department: 9 degree programs discontinued unanimously including Gender Studies, Urban Planning and Applied Math
Notes: Board of Trustees voted unanimously June 25 (two separate motions) to discontinue all 9 programs identified by Provost Lorenzo Smith. Programs discontinued: BA Gender, Women's and Sexuality Studies (CIP 05.0207); BA Urban and Regional Planning (CIP 4.0201); BA International Affairs (CIP 45.0901); BA Applied Technology; BA Data Science (CIP 11.0401); BA English as a Second Language (CIP 13.1401); BA Early Childhood and Special Education (CIP 13.1001); MA Interdisciplinary Studies; MS Applied Mathematics (CIP 27.0301). Faculty Senate recommended saving GWSS, Urban Planning, International Affairs, and Applied Technology — overruled by provost and president. Provost Smith recommended all 9 discontinued June 18; President McMahan passed to board same day. Programs averaged under 10 graduates/year over past 5 years. Mathematics and Anthropology removed from original 11-program list early due to enrollment projections. Urban Planning had highest declared incoming freshmen: 2. Many courses will continue as minors. Current declared majors may complete degrees. Spokane Mayor Lisa Brown appeared in February in support of GWSS program — overruled. Part of second major round of EWU cuts; prior round took place 2024-25 school year. Fall 2025 enrollment: just under 10,000 students. EWU is only Spokane County-headquartered public university.

Program/Department: 20 positions eliminated to close $6.5M FY2027 budget deficit
Notes: [staff] Board approved FY2027 budget June 23 eliminating 20 currently occupied positions out of ~900 full-time employees (~2.2% of workforce). Budget gap: $4M projected revenue increase vs $10.5M expense increase = $6.5M deficit. Working group of faculty, staff and administrators found $12.9M in total cuts (exceeding deficit). Missouri facing $1.5-2B state general revenue shortfall; higher ed leadership advised to prepare for at least 10% state appropriations cut for FY2028 — equal to ~$5M for SEMO. President Hodson contract extended through June 30, 2030. Board also approved stadium Phase II design contract with OSPORTS (designs due December 2026). No academic programs eliminated in this round.

Program/Department: Health Sciences Division dissolved — 28 positions eliminated in final integration phase
Notes: [staff] Health Sciences Division administrative structure permanently dissolved effective August 7, 2026 — final phase of year-long realignment. ~28 positions eliminated. All programs folded directly into existing university units: Interprofessional Clinical and Professional Skills Center + Center for Transformative Interprofessional Healthcare + Arizona Area Health Education Centers + Indigenous health programs → under new provost-selected supervisors. Clinical and Translational Science Institute + Arizona Center for Accelerated Biomedical Innovation → Office of Research and Partnerships. Clinical Placements and Partnerships → Mel and Enid Zuckerman College of Public Health. Interprofessional K-12 Initiatives + All of Us Research Program → College of Medicine Tucson. Room scheduling → Office of the Registrar. Interim VP Jennifer Barton returning to research (cancer imaging tools). Health Sciences budget $48.6M following 18% cut last year — unclear how funds will be allocated post-restructuring. Provost Prelock: "reduce administrative redundancy and build a leaner structure." HR offering affected employees assistance finding other UA positions. No academic programs eliminated — all health sciences programs continue under new administrative homes.

Program/Department: 30+ positions eliminated including 14 faculty — 401(k) matching discontinued to save $4.4M
Notes: 30+ total employees severed including 14 of ~200 faculty members. 401(k) matching program also discontinued. Saves $4.4M against $5M projected budget shortfall. President Brian McAulay announced June 16 via email calling decisions "difficult but necessary." Root cause: chiropractic flagship program placed on CCE probation in 2024 for 77% licensing exam pass rate (below 80% threshold) — probation lifted January 2026 after 100% winter pass rate. But enrollment disruption persists: 2,289 students fall 2025 (lowest in 10+ years), down 11% YoY; chiropractic college enrollment down 16%. 90%+ of revenue comes from tuition; chiropractic program provides 75% of operating revenue — making university extremely sensitive to enrollment shifts. Doctor of Chiropractic costs ~$200K; undergraduate ~$55K. Moody's downgraded bond rating March 2026 with "negative" outlook. 439 full-time employees fall 2024 (federal data). One of the largest chiropractic programs nationally. Marietta GA; private non-profit. Prior actions: Rosen College library at UCF closed same week in similar dynamic of post-preeminence budget pressure.

Program/Department: 31 positions eliminated across multiple units as part of budget reductions
Notes: [staff] Internal emails obtained by Cap Times confirm 31 positions being eliminated across multiple UW-Madison units. Cuts include: Division of Information Technology (DoIT) — layoffs and position eliminations; University Communications — staff reductions; Office of Sustainability — significant cuts; Wisconsin Public Media (WPM) — positions eliminated including programming staff. Additional measures: travel restrictions, hiring freezes, reduced discretionary spending. Driven by flat state funding, federal research grant reductions, and rising operational costs. Separate from the 100-160 potential Extension layoffs (WARN Act court filing, April 2026) which remain contingent on court ruling over USDA funding freeze — those are captured in a separate database entry. Chancellor Jennifer Mnookin has not yet made a formal campus-wide announcement about the full scope of cuts.

Program/Department: 7 degree and certificate programs discontinued as part of regular program review
Notes: Board of Governors approved discontinuation of 7 programs June 10: BS Computer and Information Security, MS Cyber Forensics and Security, MA Journalism, Graduate Certificates in Digital Communications, Digital Forensics, Integrated Strategic Communications, and Media Management. 4 of the 7 (Journalism MA, Digital Communications, Media Management, Integrated Strategic Communications certificates) had enrollment suspended since 2022 and were already in teach-out. Part of routine program review process. Budget deficit reduced from $28M to $10M; projected to fall below $3M over next year with help of Huron consulting firm assessing organizational alignment, revenue opportunities, and inefficiencies. Metro Tuition rate expanded to all border states by 2028 to attract out-of-state students. President Smith cited "three Ds" — demographic cliff, digital disruption, and doubt about higher ed value — as challenges Marshall is navigating.

Program/Department: Baking & Pastry Arts, Culinary Arts and Paralegal programs eliminated — 4 faculty affected
Notes: Board voted unanimously June 9 to eliminate 3 programs: Baking and Pastry Arts, Culinary Arts, and Paralegal. 3 faculty in food programs laid off via reduction-in-force vote (Culinary Arts Professor Emily Wallace, Baking and Pastry Arts Professor Melanie Shelton, Culinary Arts Professor J.P. Downey-McCarthy); Paralegal faculty member retired (4 total). Food programs cost college $618K/year combined; cited low enrollment and low earning potential for graduates — no formal education required for entry-level positions. Affected students may complete programs via teach-out. Nearly 20 students and community members spoke in favor of food programs at board meeting. Professors argued for restructuring not elimination — proposed changes would save $250K/year and create self-sustaining budget; board did not adopt. Programs described as serving marginalized communities including students of color, queer and trans students, neurodivergent students. Professor Wallace has already found new job at Bremerton School District launching culinary program for high school students. $3.4M-$4M budget shortfall driven by tuition not keeping pace with salary/benefits growth — personnel costs now 83% of budget. President Timothy Stokes called decisions "incredibly difficult."

Program/Department: Political Science, Childhood Development and Music programs eliminated under SB 185 financial exigency law
Notes: Board of Regents approved elimination of 3 programs June 8: Political Science, Childhood Development, and several Music areas. Affected students offered teach-out plans. CPE Academic and Strategic Initiatives Committee approved full recovery plan June 9. Undergraduate enrollment projected to drop 9% fall 2026 and 20% by spring 2027. Under Kentucky Senate Bill 185 (passed spring 2026 declaring KSU in "financial exigency"): university transitioning to polytechnic institution focused on STEM and healthcare; limited to 10 academic areas of study (applied sciences, health sciences, natural sciences, humanities, engineering and technology). Many liberal arts programs shifting online and taught entirely by adjunct faculty. New admission requirements: minimum 2.5 GPA + 18 ACT composite score. Stricter tuition enforcement: students with $1,000+ outstanding balance for 30+ days barred from enrolling; debts referred to KY Dept of Revenue; federal/state tax refunds intercepted for debts over $1,000 past 60 days. President granted authority to terminate any employee including tenured faculty with 30 days notice. Two active lawsuits seeking to block SB 185; judge allowed academic changes to continue pending final ruling. Kentucky's only public HBCU; founded 1886; land grant institution. Polytechnic restructuring does not change HBCU status. CPE President Thompson: "We are not just killing programs — we are reengineering liberal arts to work with our polytechnic focus."

Program/Department: 5 majors and 4 minors sunsetted plus 15 voluntary separations under Doane Forward plan
Notes: Majors sunsetted fall 2027: New Media, Strategic Communication, Policy and Values, Ethics and Interfaith Studies, Human Relations. Minors sunsetted: Film, Journalism, Communicating Quantitative Information, Communication/Environmental Communication. ~80 students affected on Crete campus and online — all may finish current pathways. 15 faculty/staff took voluntary separation packages; teaching faculty retained through 2026-27 to complete teach-out. Savings amount not disclosed; departments asked to prepare 13-20% budget reduction drafts (April 2026). Part of "Doane Forward" 6-month strategic plan developed with stakeholder input. Simultaneously building new innovation center covering engineering, business, AI, computer science, data analytics and mathematics — developed with input from CEOs. New 4-year engineering + 1-year MBA pathway in development. President Hughes cited national trend: "every month, a school like Doane will close." Private liberal arts institution in Crete NE. Also: Nebraska Wesleyan University (not in database) eliminated 14 staff and reduced 3 positions to part-time in October 2025.

Program/Department: Westminster Conservatory band and orchestral instrument departments discontinued after 56 years
Notes: Westminster Conservatory of Music (Princeton) band and orchestral instrument departments discontinued — all instructors effectively let go including 29-year clarinet/saxophone faculty Ken Ellison, 48-year flute faculty Amy Wolfe, 20-year piano/assistant director Marianne Lauffer, and others. Piano, voice, recorder, honors music, Opera Outings, and Westminster Community Orchestra programs relocated to Rider's Lawrence Township campus (not discontinued). Band and orchestral instrument instruction (strings, woodwinds, brass, percussion) eliminated entirely — no space at Lawrence Township campus. Conservatory founded 1970 on former Westminster Choir College campus; part of Rider since 1992. Municipality of Princeton acquired the 22-acre campus April 2025; stated it was not consulted and learned of decision simultaneously with general public June 8. Decision described as "purely operational" by Rider Senior Associate Dean Vodlicka — spending significantly more than revenue on the Princeton-based programs. Part of $21.8M deficit Rider has faced in recent years. Faculty given opportunity to meet with administration June 9; Rider exploring partnerships with other area organizations to continue private lessons.

Program/Department: 40 positions eliminated and athletic scholarships reduced to cut $10M in spending
Notes: 40 total positions eliminated as part of $10M spending reduction target. No major academic programs eliminated; biblical languages major discontinued; College of Online Learning restructured to integrate with main degree programs (May 2026). Athletic scholarships reduced — average scholarships for student athletes to near $16K starting 2026-27. University remains on federal watch list for shaky financial stability. Assemblies of God-affiliated institution; ~2,000 students; Springfield MO. Prior rounds: 2023 saw 44 employees affected (32 retirement buyouts + 12 layoffs); 2014 saw 25 positions cut in post-consolidation restructuring with Assemblies of God Theological Seminary and Central Bible College. Raised $117M+ in "Here Now" fundraising campaign over 4 years; invested in AGFinancial Arena and Walther Hall renovation. Discontinued employee tuition discount for dependents in 2025-26. Restructuring part of broader effort to grow enrollment using freed-up funds.

Program/Department: MA Literature and MA Economics eliminated; Chinese Studies minor paused
Notes: MA in Literature (CIP 23.0101) eliminated — only 8 students enrolled at time of closure, down from 16 in 2018. Final cohort completing degrees; no new admissions. MA in Economics (CIP 45.0601) also eliminated. Moratorium on minors in Chinese Studies (~10 students) and Irish Studies (~7 students). Students in eliminated programs describe feeling abandoned mid-degree with limited job market options for humanities graduates. One student said she feels her degree is now "worthless on paper." Faculty acknowledged the difficult position students are in but noted financial pressures left no alternative. Originally proposed January 28, 2026 pending Faculty Senate and Commissioner of Higher Education approval — both approvals now confirmed. Part of broader UM response to $18M FY27 budget shortfall; university also cut fewer than 10 staff via layoffs. UM MFA in Creative Writing continues unaffected. UMaine System approved 10 other program suspensions/eliminations this fiscal year across other campuses.

Program/Department: 11 positions eliminated campuswide amid enrollment and cost pressures
Notes: [staff] 11 employees laid off across several departments and programs campuswide. University cited "operational and financial pressures" including enrollment realities and rising costs. Affected employees informed directly and privately. Simultaneous dining services transition to Sodexo Campus partnership (effective June 1) impacted 45 workers — ~90% hired by Sodexo. These are separate from the 11 direct layoffs. Private university founded 1836; ~1,843 students; $203M endowment. President Mark Zupan. Part of broader NY private institution financial pressures.

Program/Department: 400-460 positions cut; four colleges consolidated into two
Notes: 15% of full-time workforce laid off — 400-460 total positions eliminated through layoffs and vacant position cuts. Layoff notices handed out June 2, 2026. Four colleges consolidated into two: Eugene Lang + New School for Social Research merged into one unit; Parsons + College of Performing Arts + Schools of Media merged into second unit. PhD admissions paused across nearly all doctoral programs for 2026-27 including sociology, philosophy, economics, politics. Student medical services gutted. Prior actions: 7% reduction via voluntary buyouts (Dec 2025); 40% of full-time faculty received voluntary separation/early retirement offers (169 academics — AAUP called it largest attempted faculty firing in the nation); S&P downgraded bond rating February 2026 citing deep deficits. Deficit variously reported as $48M structural deficit / $60M operating deficit. Mandate from board: balanced budget by FY2028. 20% enrollment decline since 2021. Parsons + College of Performing Arts alumni rallied repeatedly throughout year. Full-time faculty facing 15% reduction. President Joel Towers; Provost Richard Kessler. Originally in database from March 2026 Hyperallergic article when status was rumor.

Program/Department: 16 positions eliminated — roughly 1% of workforce — as part of strategic restructuring
Notes: [staff] ~16 employees laid off week of June 2 — roughly 1% of ~1,600-person total workforce. University may also eliminate additional vacant positions as restructuring continues. Part of broader reallocation toward functions aligned with long-term strategy. Provost announced required 15% budget cut for Academic Affairs by end of FY2028 (November 2025). Library collections budget decreasing from $2.6M to lower level as part of same cuts. Driven by federal and state funding cuts, enrollment shifts, and industry demand changes. Specialist STEM institution in Golden CO; known for engineering, applied sciences, and energy research. Separate from CSU Fort Collins ($35.8M cuts) and CSU Pueblo (9 positions) also in database — all part of Colorado higher ed funding squeeze.

Program/Department: 36 nonfaculty staff eliminated — 15% of nonfaculty workforce in second round of cuts
Notes: [staff] 26 full-time + 10 part-time nonfaculty staff eliminated June 1 — 15% of nonfaculty workforce. Saves ~$3.5M. Combined with faculty cuts ($3M) and contract/other savings ($1M+) = ~$7.5M of $10M goal reached. Additional savings: Berman Museum annual funding cut from $600K to $300K; advertising and cleaning contracts changed; software changes; consultants eliminated; annual alumni awards ceremony ended; family and homecoming weekends combined; staff credit card purchasing tightened. President Graml: "We have to be leaner in order to really focus on the student mission." Running total of Ursinus cuts in 2025-26: 29 faculty + 36 staff = 65 total positions eliminated.

Program/Department: Center for a Regenerative Future closed after 3 years of budget-driven decline
Notes: Center for a Regenerative Future (CRF, formerly Center for Sustainability) closing June 30 after 3 years of budget-driven decline. Formerly housed thrift store, bike shop, gear garage, food pantry, climate cafes, community dinners, graduate gown recycling, and 40-student paid internship program (now reduced to 2 interns). Undergraduate program director position cut spring 2024 triggering collapse of thrift store. Bike shop and gear garage absorbed by Basecamp. Food pantry restructured under Student Affairs and Inclusive Excellence. Part of DU administration effort to reduce $10M from non-academic units amid $20-30M budget deficit. Faculty senate passed no-confidence vote in Chancellor Haefner (May 2026). Remaining staff hosting "Living Funeral" June 5 to redistribute materials to campus organizations.

Program/Department: 32 academic advising positions eliminated as part of advising system redesign
Notes: [staff] 32 academic advising positions eliminated as part of university advising system redesign. Notably some employees were previously laid off, then rehired, and are now losing their jobs again in this second round. University stated "any reductions in force are difficult." Cuts are administrative staff positions — advisers who support student academic planning and degree completion. No academic programs eliminated.

Program/Department: 66 positions eliminated including 29 layoffs to address $20M structural deficit
Notes: 29 employees laid off + 37 vacant positions eliminated (66 total). Reorganization follows 2-year Huron Consulting Group assessment and Operation Excellence Initiative. Work groups identified $18M in savings across academic programs, compensation/benefits, technology and endowment. Prior signals: hiring freeze Dec 2025-May 2026 for vacant positions; 2025 benefit cuts; graduate revenue below projections; insurance and utility costs rose sharply. Second-largest private university in Maryland (~4,000 undergrad, 1,900 grad). Jesuit institution. President Sawyer said Loyola is "well-positioned for the future." Part of Maryland higher ed wave: UMD College Park (150 jobs), Bowie State ($18M deficit), UMB (60 positions), Morgan State all cutting simultaneously due to $111M state funding reduction.

Program/Department: 6 tenured faculty laid off — fourth round of cuts since January 2025
Notes: Wednesday May 27 layoffs fell on 6 tenured faculty in School of Communication and Culture and School of Design. Fourth round of faculty layoffs since January 2025 — prior rounds: 48 full-time faculty total (32 tenured) since Jan 2025, plus 70 staff in 2024. Part of ongoing effort to close $40M+ deficit amid declining enrollment. Layoff notices described as coming without prior warning to affected faculty. Running total since 2024: 70 staff + 54 faculty laid off. President Bolton simultaneously hiring new senior leadership (5 new VP-level hires in spring 2026) — Chronicle noted tension between cuts and new hires. Admin restructured May 2 into 5-dean oversight model. No further rounds ruled out.

Program/Department: BA in Religious Studies eliminated; multiple zero-enrollment minors and certificates closed
Notes: UH System Board of Regents approved closure of BA in Religious Studies at May 22 quarterly meeting. 15 students enrolled; 5 not actively pursuing degree. Failed to meet Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board threshold of 25 graduates over 5 years. Religious studies minor remains; religion courses continue in core curriculum and as electives. No faculty layoffs — professors retained. Part of Texas SB 37 compliance review: additional closure of multiple minors and certificates across UH System (UH, UH-Clear Lake) with zero enrollments for past 5 years. Simultaneously approved new BA in Philosophy, Politics and Economics and new BS in Biological Sciences. Provost Chase cited statewide and national trend of declining religion/biblical studies enrollment. Prior language program cuts at UH: German, Italian, French (over past 10 years). Board also delegated expanded contracting authority to Chancellor Khator.

Program/Department: Men's and women's tennis programs discontinued following coach departure
Notes: [staff] Men's tennis ended immediately; women's tennis continues through 2026-27 then discontinued. Longtime head coach Bert Poole departing for another coaching opportunity — his exit triggered the decision to end both programs. Division III institution; member of ODAC (Old Dominion Athletic Conference). Women's tennis recently fell 4-0 to No. 13 Washington and Lee in ODAC championship.

Program/Department: 11 core faculty and ~40 instructor positions eliminated to address structural deficit
Notes: President Paul Burkhardt sent letter to staff and faculty announcing elimination of 11 core faculty positions and ~40 instructor jobs to correct long-term structural operating deficit. Burkhardt acknowledged "these sorts of reductions are very difficult, and they cause suffering." Separate April 17, 2026 announcement introduced tuition reset for fall 2026 (lower per-credit rate for new students, flat for current) and new Ponderosa Plan strategic framework for long-term sustainability. New online and low-residency programs added simultaneously. Buddhist-inspired nonsectarian liberal arts institution founded 1974; ~1,100 students. Known as birthplace of modern mindfulness movement.

Program/Department: 21 programs and minors eliminated — second round of cuts in 3 years to close $8.1M deficit
Notes: 10 undergraduate programs, 4 graduate programs, and 7 minors discontinued. Named programs: Mathematics (BA/BS), Physics (BA/BS), Economics (BA/BS), and others. 171 total students affected (111 majors + 60 minor students) — less than 5% of total enrollment; only 25 are incoming fall 2026 students. All current and incoming accepted students can complete degrees via teach-out. Second major round of cuts: prior 2024 round eliminated 12 programs including French, Spanish, Philosophy, and Early Childhood Education. $8.1M structural deficit being addressed through program cuts and enrollment growth strategy. Deficit reduced by nearly half since 2023. Graduate enrollment up ~50% over 3 years driven by new programs (Clinical Mental Health Counseling: 65 students). Courses required for other majors will continue to be offered. President Stephen H. Kolison Jr. cited need to focus resources on high-demand growing programs.

Program/Department: Residential in-person classes suspended; 167 employees laid off
Notes: WARN Act notice filed April 1 for 167 employees (110 full-time, 57 adjunct/part-time) effective June 1 — ~34% of workforce. Board of Trustees voted May 15 to suspend all residential undergraduate in-person classes while continuing online programs. Students given 48 hours notice to vacate campus housing. ~350 traditional undergrad students told to find alternative arrangements. Graduate and online programs continue. University simultaneously exploring sale of carbon capture patent and seeking investor group to acquire institution. President Dempsey said board hopes to reopen traditional programs fall 2026 but could not guarantee it. Indiana Commission for Higher Education notified; transfer pathways being developed. Private General Baptist institution founded 1885. Financial collapse attributed to years of enrollment decline, deferred maintenance, and failed fundraising campaigns.

Program/Department: 3 programs discontinued and 2 paused amid 7% budget reduction and Washington funding crisis
Notes: Programs discontinued: Administrative Office Systems, Paralegal, Multimedia. Programs paused fall 2026 pending enrollment strategy review: Automotive Service Technician, Family Life Education.
