Construction Trades program (previously under review) retained with updated curriculum, expanded lab, new equipment, and community donations. Furloughs planned July 2026 for exempt and classified employees earning $90K+/year as one-year stabilization measure. College already reduced overall budget ~7% over past year including closure of Fort Worden campus. New programs proceeding despite cuts: Dental Hygiene, K-8 Teacher Education, and mobile workforce training — all supported by external grants, partnerships, and philanthropy. Driven by rising operating costs and Washington state community college funding challenges. President Suzy Ames said review involved Board of Trustees, President's Cabinet, faculty leadership, and employees. Serves Clallam and Jefferson counties.

Program/Department: 35 programs eliminated and 10 faculty laid off to address $20M deficit
Notes: 35 total programs eliminated: 28 undergraduate majors and minors + 7 graduate programs. Named majors cut: Health Education, Economics, Human Resources, International Business, Mild/Moderate Educational Needs, Music Theory, Physics, Sociology, Sustainability. 10 faculty laid off as a result. Deficit grew from initial $3M estimate to $20M. Second major round: prior cuts in late 2024 saw 35 faculty/staff laid off or offered buyouts (~7% of teaching base). Former faculty cited toxic work environment, HR complaints not followed up, secretive reasoning for cuts. President Lee Fisher announced via May 9 email to faculty/staff following May 8 board meeting. Private liberal arts and conservatory institution in Berea, OH.

Program/Department: 3 majors eliminated and 66 positions cut to close $5M deficit after Deloitte review
Notes: [staff] Board voted May 9 to approve restructuring plan. 3 academic programs permanently eliminated: Music, International Studies, and Gender/Sexuality/Women's Studies (125 combined student majors). Creative Writing merged into English department. 9 other academic units consolidated. ~66 total positions eliminated: faculty in eliminated/consolidated programs + administrative restructuring. Saves $5M annually — satisfying Oregon HECC requirement for balanced long-term plan tied to $15M emergency state funding (approved February 2026). Deloitte analysis found top 3 units (business, education, psychology) represent 45% of headcount; top 10 programs = 78% of enrollment; 10 units operated at a loss. Outsourcing of administrative functions to Oregon flagship universities or third-party providers also approved. Average course enrollment minimum raised from 16 to 22 students. 56 faculty had signed letter disputing Deloitte data quality prior to vote. Board chair thanked community for input during "difficult but necessary" process. Part of Oregon higher ed funding crisis — state ranks 14th from bottom in per-FTE spending. Prior year: SOU cut 23 programs and laid off 18 employees.

Program/Department: Energy and Environmental Research Center cuts 27 positions, furloughs 13 amid federal funding delays
Notes: EERC (Energy and Environmental Research Center) at UND cut 27 positions and furloughed 13 (full or temporary basis) from ~210-person workforce. Furloughed employees may be reinstated based on operational needs and funding. Cuts driven by multi-year delays in federal funding — primarily from U.S. Dept of Energy — compounded by Trump administration spending curbs. FY2025 budget ~$85M: $40M competitive federal grants, $30M private sector, remainder state sources. COO Tom Erickson told legislators in January: "We are waiting for the funds that were promised to us over a year ago." EERC designated North Dakota's State Energy Research Center; research spans coal, oil, natural gas, biomass, carbon capture, geothermal, nuclear, and EVs. Hosted Energy Secretary Chris Wright in 2025. UND and NDSU representatives previously told legislators Trump-era spending cuts already cost ND millions in research funding.

Program/Department: New admissions suspended in some programs; overlapping degrees consolidated
Notes: UTA confirmed via email to faculty/staff and statement to WFAA that it will suspend new admissions into some programs and consolidate overlapping degree pathways in others. Changes affect fewer than 200 of 42,700+ enrolled students. All currently enrolled/admitted students can complete degrees without disruption; individualized advising and transition options will be provided. Suspending new admissions: BA in Art History, MS in Sustainable Building Technology, MS in Taxation (certificates, elective courses, and minors in these programs remain available). Consolidations/mergers: BA Chemistry → BS Chemistry, BA Geology → BS Geology, BA Mathematics → BS Mathematics, BA Theatre Arts → BFA Theatre Arts, MA Mathematics → MS Mathematics. Admissions suspended pending interdisciplinary curriculum revision: BA Anthropology, Master of Engineering, MS in Materials Science and Engineering. UTA cited faculty engagement and data-driven analysis. Review conducted by a representative faculty group. UT System Board of Regents policy "Abandonment of Academic Positions or Programs" permits the university president to eliminate programs absent financial exigency, citing low enrollment, redundancy, program quality, and student outcomes. Academic program review initiated in 2025 to align offerings with student demand, workforce needs, and long-term institutional sustainability.

Program/Department: 96 UK employees laid off due to federal grant terminations in medicine and HIV programs
Notes: 96 employees in UK College of Medicine Department of Behavioral Science and UK Healthcare HIV Program Operations laid off effective June 30 due to discontinuation of federal grant funding. UK will try to help affected employees find other positions at the university; all employees receive 60 days notice and pay per WARN Act. Separate from 926 Aramark Campus LLC dining/concessions contractor layoffs (also effective June 30) — those are third-party contractor employees, not UK staff, and Aramark/UK expect most to transition to new provider. UK ending 12-year Aramark partnership and exploring new enterprise services provider for dining and concessions.

Program/Department: $35.8M in strategic cuts including staff layoffs and 0.5% workforce reduction
Notes: CSU System board approved FY2027 budget May 7-8 with $35.8M in strategic cuts at Fort Collins campus: staff layoffs (0.5% of workforce) + $3M from eliminating vacant positions. Financial aid tied to tuition costs preserved; 3% merit raise pool maintained for faculty/staff. Driven by Colorado state budget flat-funding higher ed to close $1.5B state deficit (constitutional balanced budget requirement). Tuition for in-state students capped at 3.5% increase by state. President Parsons called flat funding "a real reduction in resources" due to cost increases. Fall headcount rose 2% to 34,096 students between 2019-2024 — one of the healthier enrollment pictures in Colorado.

Program/Department: 79 positions eliminated amid second consecutive multimillion-dollar deficit
Notes: [staff] President Aminta Breaux announced elimination of 79 total positions through reorganization, vacancy cuts, and direct layoffs — ~6% of 1,175-person workforce. Second consecutive deficit: $13.6M shortfall in prior year (resolved via hiring delays and vacant position cuts); now facing $18M deficit for 2026-27. Maryland's oldest HBCU, founded 1865. Prior year deficit addressed without layoffs; this round requires direct workforce reduction. Breaux stated decisions made "with care, thoughtfulness and deep respect for faculty, staff and students." Specific breakdown of faculty vs staff positions not disclosed in available reporting.

Program/Department: INSPIRE first-year student success program shut down due to lack of funding
Notes: [staff] INSPIRE (Incoming Student Program for Inclusion, Retention, and Excellence) shutting down after spring 2026 semester. Established 2022; served first-year students with small cohorts, GE course support, financial planning, schedule planning, and faculty/peer connections. Particularly impactful for first-generation college students. Shut down due to lack of funding amid CSU system-wide budget crisis ($1B+ projected CSU deficit for 2026-27). CSUEB enrollment down ~26% since 2016. Mock funeral protest held by students and staff on campus. Separate ongoing cuts include Theater and Dance department merger/closure threat (1,400+ signature petition), Art program course cuts, and ART 242 elimination affecting graduating students.

Program/Department: 4 programs eliminated under Ohio SB1 mandate, 19 total cut since 2024
Notes: Most recent round eliminated 4 programs: BA Public Health (merged into BS Public Health), Regional Studies graduate certificate (0 enrolled), School Nurse graduate certificate (0 enrolled), MA International Relations (declining enrollment; new track in MPA being developed). Part of ongoing Ohio SB1 compliance requiring elimination of programs with fewer than 15 graduates over 3 years. WSU previously eliminated 15 programs under SB1 including BA African-American Studies, BA Women and Gender Studies, BA Philosophy, BA Chemistry, and others. 5 new programs approved simultaneously: BS Accelerated Health Sciences, STEM MBA, Classical Cultures minor, Manufacturing and Logistics minor, Operations and Data Analytics minor. Provost James Denniston cited enrollment trends, workforce needs, incoming student interests, HS pathways, and peer institution offerings as decision factors. Spring 2026 commencement: 1,650+ graduates, up YoY in College of Liberal Arts and Lake Campus (+20%).

Program/Department: Permanent institution closure after 43 years due to enrollment challenges
Notes: [staff] Physical campus at 1725 E. David Road closed May 4, 2026; instruction ends June 2; permanent closure June 23, 2026. Founded 1983 by Tim Potter as School of Advertising Art; rebranded to Modern College of Design in 2017-18 following $6M expansion adding 23,000 sq ft. President Jessica Barry (since 2007, purchased college 2013) cited inability to support operations due to enrollment challenges despite efforts to evolve. ~211 students enrolled (federal data); 92% acceptance rate; 59% graduation rate. Offered bachelor's and associate degrees in graphic design. Record enrollment of 214 in 2024-25 school year — closure came despite recent enrollment growth. No summer semester; summer tuition/fees to be refunded. Transfer agreements with local/online design programs being developed. Virtual commencement June 7; diplomas mailed after. Students unable to complete may apply for Closed School Discharge (federal student loan forgiveness). Career services available through June 23. Building valued at ~$3.8M per county records.

Program/Department: 19 positions eliminated across IT Services and Luddy School of Informatics
Notes: [staff] 13 IT Services (UITS) positions eliminated May 1 per VP Kendra Ketchum email — driven by need to align resources with university priorities and ensure long-term financial sustainability. 6 additional Luddy School of Informatics, Computing and Engineering positions eliminated May 29 per Dean Joanna Millunchick email — part of school restructuring to align with evolving university priorities. 19 total confirmed cuts; university declined to confirm broader scope despite social media reports of additional departmental cuts. IU policy requires 30 days written notice; WARN Act 60-day notice applies if total exceeds 50. No WARN filing on Indiana DWD website as of publication. Separate from Indiana HEA 1001 program cuts (April 2026) also in database. Also: IU-licensed public media station WFIU/WTIU cut 4 full-time + 14 part-time positions the same week.

Program/Department: Up to 45 staff layoffs to close $18M FY2027 budget shortfall
Notes: [staff] President Diacon announced up to 45 layoffs in April 30 "Talk with Todd" campus address; notices going out in coming weeks pending FY2027 budget board approval. VP budgets cut 5-10%. $18M shortfall driven by expected state funding reduction, anticipated enrollment decline, inflation, and significant drop in international students due to federal visa policy changes. 2% raise for all non-union employees also announced. KSU has been reducing budget gradually for 10+ years. Strong enrollment continues in College of Aeronautics and Engineering and fashion design. Total Ohio public university enrollment today roughly same as 2005 but state support (inflation-adjusted) is 27% lower. Diacon cited Penn State (50 major closures), UMD (150 positions), ECU ($25M shortfall), and Clemson as peer institutions facing similar pressures.

Program/Department: Radcliffe Institute staff layoffs and role reductions
Notes: Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study laid off 4 employees, shifted 3 to part-time, and eliminated 8 vacant positions (15 total roles affected). Institute employs ~100 people. Announced by Dean Tomiko Brown-Nagin via Wednesday email citing "wide range of federal actions targeting Harvard, cost pressures, and market volatility." Harvard central administration directed all units to pursue "structural cuts." Follows prior hiring freeze, salary freeze for non-union employees, and vacant role eliminations. Radcliffe endowment-dependent (86% of revenue). Harvard reported $113M deficit in FY2025 on $6.7B revenue — first deficit since pandemic. New 8% endowment tax (Big Beautiful Bill) projected to cost Harvard $200M+/year. DOJ lawsuit filed alleging Title VI Civil Rights Act violations. FAS departments already asked to plan for up to 20% budget cuts. Brown-Nagin noted uncertainty will last "years, not months."

Program/Department: 44 academic programs discontinued as part of $25M savings plan
Notes: 44 total programs discontinued: 33 voluntarily identified by faculty/administrators + 11 recommended by APRO oversight committee last year. Named programs include: BA Sociology (CIP 45.1101), MAED Middle Grades, MS Software Engineering (CIP 14.0903), MS Sustainable Tourism and Hospitality, PB Sustainable Tourism and Hospitality, Minor Ethnic Studies, Minor Physics (CIP 40.0801), Minor Speech and Hearing, PB Gerontology, BS Family and Consumer Sciences, PB Medical Family Therapy. Currently enrolled students may finish degrees via teach-out. Part of 3-year $25M savings target; first-year goal of $6M+ already exceeded. Additional restructuring: new College of Health and Human Sciences created, library services changed, financial aid and summer school operations updated. Chancellor Philip Rogers cited long-term financial sustainability. Full APRO report at fiscalhealth.ecu.edu.

Program/Department: Susan Polgar Institute for Chess Excellence (SPICE) program eliminated
Notes: [staff] SPICE (Susan Polgar Institute for Chess Excellence) eliminated after 14 years at Webster (moved from Texas Tech 2012). Program accolades: 2 world championships, 3 Olympiad gold medals, 90+ national titles, 10 Pan-American Intercollegiate championships, 7 Final Four titles; just won 2026 Pan-Am for 13th consecutive President's Cup berth. Head coach GM Liem Le confirmed departure April 30. Program cost $1M+/year from operating budget; university says it raised $0 in outside endowments in 14 years. Reasons cited: unsustainable operating cost during years of losses, enrollment declines (Webster campus enrollment declined by half), and Trump-era visa restrictions (most team members attended on visas; Webster ranks 2nd in Missouri for enrollment decline due to visa restrictions). University posted first net-positive revenue in 10+ years after recent restructuring; chess savings to contribute to fiscal year goals. Program founder Susan Polgar publicly disputed university's account, saying she was never contacted and could have launched fundraising campaign; called closure equivalent to Alabama eliminating football. Program alumni include GMs Wesley So, Ray Robson, and Awonder Liang.

Program/Department: 9 FTE staff positions eliminated to close $2.4M structural deficit
Notes: CSU Pueblo eliminated equivalent of ~9 full-time staff positions plus closed 8 vacant positions, reorganized units, and cut athletics budget by $1M to close $2.4M structural deficit. In-state tuition raised 3.5%, out-of-state 5%. Announced by President Rhonda Epper in April 29 budget update. Enrollment fell 3.2% to 6,851 students between 2019-2024. Epper cited "tight competitive market and some negative narratives about the value of higher education" alongside budgetary constraints. Part of broader Colorado higher ed flat-funding crisis driving cuts across the state system.

Program/Department: Men's NCAA Division I tennis program discontinued
Notes: Men's tennis discontinued effective end of spring 2026 semester. 8-member roster (2025-26); 5 are seniors with completed eligibility; 3 remaining eligible for transfer portal (opens May 4). Scholarships honored through degree completion. Head coach Maja Kovacek continues coaching women's team (which won MVC championship 2026). Program competed in Summit League for 9 years after MVC dropped men's tennis in 2017; prior 36 years in MVC. Finished 2026 season 9-14, eliminated in Summit League Championship semifinals. Third Division I school to cut tennis in 5 days (after Arkansas April 24 and SLU April 27). Reason: thorough analysis of multiple factors per AD Jeri Beggs; no additional details disclosed. Women's program unaffected.

Program/Department: Men's and women's NCAA Division I tennis programs discontinued
Notes: Men's (est. 1975) and women's (est. 1976) NCAA Division I tennis programs discontinued effective immediately following completion of 2025-26 season at Atlantic 10 Conference Championships. 19 total student-athletes (10 men, 9 women); 5 graduating spring 2026; remaining 14 eligible for immediate transfer portal entry under discontinuation-of-sport exception. 2 coaching positions eliminated: head coach James Tobin (full-time, 2nd year) and assistant Emilien Burnel (part-time); staff member Lizzie Barlow also thanked. No on-campus facility; teams played at Dwight Davis Tennis Center and Missouri Athletic Club West. Operating expenses: $173,199 for 2023-24 per Dept. of Education filing. SLU drops to 16 Division I sports (minimum 14 required). First programs cut since men's and women's golf in 2006. Part of national wave: University of Arkansas also dropped tennis same week. Driven by NIL/revenue-sharing era budget pressures.

Program/Department: Up to 150 positions eliminated amid 10% state funding cut and federal research losses
Notes: Hiring freeze effective immediately April 27; up to 150 positions eliminated through layoffs, retirements and vacancy eliminations. No new positions created until at least June 30; positions at offer stage may proceed. Travel restricted; contracted services require CFO approval; capital projects limited to essential operations. Driven by 10%+ state funding reduction ($111M cut across University System of Maryland to close $3.3B state deficit) + reduced federal support + rising costs. Total state funding $2.21B for FY2026. UMD among 12 USM schools absorbing cuts alongside UMB (60 positions), UMES, Morgan State, Towson (hiring pause), Bowie State ($18M deficit). Part of systemic Maryland higher ed funding crisis.

Program/Department: Four degree programs eliminated amid $4.5M budget cuts
Notes: Board of Regents approved elimination of 4 degrees: MS in Education - Higher Education (opposed by Regent Wilmot); BA in Modern Languages - German emphasis (CIP 16.0501); BM in Music Business emphasis; BA in Education - Modern Languages 7-12 German Teaching Endorsement. Chosen for low/declining enrollment and poor long-term viability. ~19 faculty roles cut via voluntary separations, eliminations, and unfilled openings. Additional $2.3M in operational/administrative reductions including graduate assistant reductions and vacating buildings. Part of $40M+ NU system-wide reductions; UNK's share proportional at $4.5M. Enrolled students may finish degrees via teach-out. Third round of UNK program cuts since 2023 (theatre and others eliminated then). UNL separately had 4 departments cut in December 2025.

Program/Department: College closing permanently at end of spring 2026
Notes: Governing board voted to permanently close at end of spring 2026 term. Founded 1946 by Sisters of Saint Anne; Catholic liberal arts institution known for music and art. Enrollment 1,202 as of fall 2024, down 16.6% since 2019. $18.4M long-term debt as of June 2025; endowment assets under $1.4M (all donor-restricted); investments fell ~80% in FY2025. Despite $2M in cost cuts, 7.5% spring enrollment increase, improved fall deposits, and fundraising beating projections, the progress was insufficient. Massachusetts Dept of Higher Education flagged as closure risk in early April 2026 citing inability to verify sufficient resources. Had explored mergers, partnerships, and alternative revenue streams before board vote. Transfer agreements in place with 5 regional colleges. Employees laid off in waves by role. Announcement made on 80th anniversary of founding.

Program/Department: Men's and women's tennis programs
Notes: Men's and women's tennis programs discontinued effective end of spring 2026 season. Announced by AD Hunter Yurachek; approved by Chancellor Charles Robinson. Men's team (16-14, 3-11 SEC) coached by Jay Udwadia; women's team (14-14, 3-12 SEC) coached by Tucker Clary — both coaches lose positions. Arkansas will be the only SEC member without a women's tennis team; Missouri is the only SEC member without men's tennis. Arkansas drops to 17 sponsored sports, just above NCAA FBS minimum of 16. Current student-athletes' scholarships honored through degree completion; transfer portal assistance offered. Driven by inability to fund programs at SEC-competitive level amid House v. NCAA settlement revenue-sharing pressures and NIL costs. Arkansas reported $195.8M operating revenues and $184M expenses in FY2025 but is among bottom five SEC NIL spenders. Future of on-campus Billingsley Tennis Center undecided.

Program/Department: All varsity sports discontinued
Notes: [staff] All varsity sports discontinued effective fall 2026 except esports: men's and women's basketball, men's and women's cross country, men's and women's soccer, and women's volleyball eliminated. 13 coaching positions cut this month; no full-time staff affected (coaches with full-time roles retain them). Saves ~$351K annually. 130 total student-athletes; 62 in esports (retained). 68 non-esports athletes affected. Students informed after enrollment deadlines had passed, sparking petition and pushback. College will expand intramural, club sports and wellness programs; women's flag football club retained. Part of broader $5M deficit mitigation for 2026-27; separate actions include 87 staff layoffs, 41 vacant position cuts, 2 faculty retrenchments, and 15 academic program restructurings/eliminations. $128M operating budget adopted April 7. New president Daniel Lufkin begins June 2026.

Program/Department: 3 graduate programs approved for closure by Iowa Board of Regents
Notes: 3 graduate programs approved for closure by Iowa Board of Regents: MA in Psychology (suspended Fall 2024; no enrolled students), Professional Science Master's in Industrial Mathematics (lost lead faculty 2021; no students since Fall 2019), and a third graduate program (not named in available reporting). Part of board-mandated low-enrollment review (graduate threshold: 10 or fewer students). Financial savings described as minimal. Current enrolled students may finish degrees; no new admissions.

Program/Department: 7 programs approved for elimination by Iowa Board of Regents
Notes: 7 programs approved for elimination by Iowa Board of Regents: BA in African American Studies (CIP 05.0201), BA in Classical Languages, BA in Gender Women's and Sexuality Studies (CIP 05.0207), BA in Italian (CIP 16.0902), BA in Russian (CIP 16.0402), BS in Applied Physics (CIP 40.0801), and MA in African American World Studies (suspended since 2021; no enrolled students for 5 years). Also dissolves two admin units: African American Studies Program and Dept of Gender Women's and Sexuality Studies in College of Liberal Arts and Sciences. Minors in African American and women's studies will continue. French program exempted after faculty grew enrollment above 30. UI found 13 undergrad and 16 grad programs underenrolled but only requested closure of 7. Financial savings described as minimal by regents.

Program/Department: Gender and Sexuality Center closed
Notes: Director position (vacant since Pat Tetreault 2024 retirement, budgeted $102K) eliminated. Remaining staff absorbed into Student Culture and Community under Office of Student Life, relocating to Jackie Gaughan Multicultural Center fall 2026. GSC established 2023 via merger of LGBTQA+ Center and Women's Center. Services redistributed: safer sex kits to University Health Center; menstrual products to Husker Pantry; Lavender Closet to Husker Closet; library content to University Library. Monthly STI drop-in testing discontinued entirely. Follows August 2024 elimination of UNL Office of Diversity and Inclusion. Part of broader NU system DEI restructuring.

Program/Department: Board voted 4-3 to close two degree programs
Notes: Board voted 4-3 to close two degree programs: Criminal Justice (15 students; program supervisor said it generates $100K/year and enrollment was increasing) and Health Information Management (59 students; teach-out arrangement with Klamath Community College). Part of $4.2M budget cuts package for 2026-27 to rebuild ending fund balance to 10% of general fund (currently projected to drop to 3.1% without action). Supervisors of both programs publicly disputed the rationale, calling the process flawed and claiming the programs operate in the black. Student government president criticized lack of student input. College also facing $550K shortfall in current fiscal year. Three-year mitigation plan overall.

Program/Department: About 25 Cal Athletics marketing and communications staff laid off
Notes: Cal Athletics laid off ~25 staff in marketing, athletic communications and creative services units, effective early June 2026. Framed as "complete redefinition" of external operations transitioning to new "Strawberry Creek Studios" revenue generation model. Driven by $24.3M projected shortfall for 2024-25 fiscal year and broader college sports landscape changes (conference realignment, transfer portal, NIL). Co-ADs Jenny Simon-O'Neill and Jay Larson announced cuts April 11. Athletics department action; no academic programs affected. New football coach Tosh Lupoi hired December 2025.

Program/Department: Staff cuts plus 41 vacant positions eliminated; York campus buildings sold
Notes: Additionally cutting 41 already-vacant positions. Driven by flat state appropriations (3 consecutive years), 1.8% projected enrollment decline, and 11% rising healthcare costs. York campus buildings being sold. Budget deficit projected near $10M without intervention.

Institution: Aviator College of Aeronautical Science and Technology
Program/Department: Main campus in Fort Pierce, FL closed
Notes: [staff] Main campus in Fort Pierce, FL closed April 15, 2026 with 40-50 layoffs (instructors, administrators, facilities staff). Students notified April 9 — just 6 days before closure. ~260 students enrolled fall 2024. Programs offered: 1-year commercial pilot ($68K+) and 2-year aviation associate degree ($115K+). Parent company attributed closure to lawsuit by former student's family, failed sale, and possible bankruptcy. Accrediting Commission of Career Schools and Colleges (ACCSC) had voted to withdraw accreditation fall 2025 following two fatal flight crashes (2023, 2024) and anonymous complaints of widespread violations including safety, faculty qualifications, enrollment agreements, and student services. As of Jan 2025, 91% of students were 100+ days behind on required flight time. College was appealing accreditation withdrawal. Kissimmee branch campus (aviation maintenance program) remains open; its accreditation withdrawal also under appeal. College said refunds to be provided and working with other schools for student transfer options.

Program/Department: 10 degree programs eliminated and 13 consolidated under Iowa Board of Regents mandate
Notes: Provost Jason Keith announced April 2 elimination of 10 degree programs and consolidation of 13 others following Iowa Board of Regents Workforce Alignment Review. Programs closed include undergrad: BS Bioinformatics and Computational Biology (CIP 26.1103), BS Environmental Studies (CIP 03.0103), BS Interdisciplinary Design, BS Religious Studies (CIP 38.0201), BS Women's and Gender Studies (CIP 05.0207); grad: MS/PhD Accounting Analytics, PhD Biophysics, PhD Energy Systems Engineering, PhD Interdisciplinary Graduate Studies, PhD Toxicology. Programs consolidated/merged: 4 physics PhDs (applied, condensed matter, high energy, nuclear) → 1 degree; Sociology + Rural Sociology → 1 graduate program; Earth Science + Geology → 1 program at each level; Rhetoric Composition and Professional Communication merged into larger program; graduate Gerontology merged into College of Health and Human Sciences program; Experiential Graphic Design consolidated into multi-credential pathway. 7 programs exempted despite low enrollment (nursing, veterinary science, math/science education). 15 programs given 2-year extension. Board of Regents approval June 15 meeting. Courses in many closed subjects continue via minors/certificates. Part of same Iowa Board of Regents review that cut programs at University of Iowa (7 programs) and University of Northern Iowa (3 programs) — both already in database. UPDATE Nov. 11, 2026: Iowa Board of Regents formally terminated 11 ISU programs (19 credentials) under the program vitality review: MS/PhD Applied Physics, Astrophysics, Condensed Matter Physics, High-Energy Physics, Nuclear Physics, Biophysics, Earth Science, Toxicology; PhD Wind Energy Science, Engineering and Policy; M.Eng. Energy Systems Engineering; BA Environmental Studies (secondary major). Graduate programs under 10 students deemed underenrolled. Currently enrolled students may finish their degrees. Regents asked for more frequent reviews and better tracking of savings. Sources: KCCI (Nov. 11, 2026), Iowa State Daily.

Program/Department: 10 programs suspended or eliminated under Indiana HEA 1001 mandate
Notes: Indiana Commission for Higher Education voted April 1 to act on 10 Ivy Tech programs. Named cuts include: associate degrees in public safety, nanotechnology, and machine repair. Ivy Tech had fewest programs flagged statewide (47 reviewed; only 10 acted upon). Part of statewide HEA 1001 compliance cutting 584 programs across 7 Indiana public universities. New Indiana law also updates Ivy Tech governance and doubles down on workforce mission.

Program/Department: MADE Program
Notes: MADE (Minorities Achieving Dreams of Excellence) student support program closing end of spring 2026 semester after 7 years. Founded 2019 as a president's office initiative to support underserved first-year students. Program coordinator Jason Perry also departing after graduation. Program offered early orientation, scholarships, monthly meetings, coaching, mentoring, study space, ambassadorships, and internships. Had 200+ students with 90%+ retention rate as of 2023. Cited reasons: UM financial crisis and broader national trend of state bills targeting DEI/equity programs. Separate from February 2026 board vote eliminating 16 minors and concentrations.

Program/Department: 4 programs suspended or eliminated under Indiana HEA 1001 mandate
Notes: Indiana Commission for Higher Education voted April 1 to act on 4 USI programs — fewest of any Indiana institution. Named cuts include: AS Early Childhood Education, MA Liberal Studies, undergraduate Electronic Business degree, Master in Social Health Services and Allied Professions. Part of statewide HEA 1001 compliance cutting 584 programs across 7 Indiana public universities.

Program/Department: 93 programs closed or paused after academic portfolio review
Notes: 93 programs sunsetted (closed or paused) out of ~460 total following 7-month academic portfolio review begun August 2025. Breakdown: 41 bachelor's degrees, 19 graduate degrees, 33 certificates (28 advanced). 55 of the 93 had zero enrolled students. 258 students affected (1.2% of 22K+ enrollment); all may complete degrees via teach-out. No positions eliminated. Affected programs include classics, ceramics, sculpture, painting, German, Italian, French, Russian, Middle Eastern studies, African American studies, digital humanities, Modern Jewish studies, and others. Driven by enrollment concentration: 34% of programs serve 80% of students. Explicitly not a cost-cutting exercise per provost. Chancellor Kent Syverud departing May 10 for University of Michigan.

Program/Department: International Studies BA, education degrees and other programs discontinued
Notes: Multiple program discontinuations and restructurings as UNO transitions to LSU New Orleans in 2026. Discontinued: BA International Studies (→ minor), BS Elementary Ed & Special Ed (Grades 1-5), MAT Elementary Ed & Special Ed (Grades 1-5), MAT Secondary Ed & Special Ed (Grades 6-12), MFA theatre-related tracks/concentrations. Restructured: BA Art History → BA Studio Art (Art History as minor); BA Film and Theatre → BA Film Arts (Theatre Arts as minor); MFA renamed. Taught out: BS Mathematics (while new BS Data Science is developed); MS Tax Accounting (existing teach-out continues). MA Arts Administration merged into MPA. Less than 2% of students affected. All faculty retained during transition. New programs under development: engineering management, hospitality and tourism, data science, healthcare management.

Program/Department: Programs suspended or eliminated under Indiana HEA 1001 mandate
Notes: Indiana Commission for Higher Education voted April 1; Vincennes University participated in statewide HEA 1001 compliance review. Specific program names not detailed in available reporting. Part of statewide action cutting 584 programs across all 7 Indiana public universities. Vincennes reported costs by cost center rather than individual program level per CHE reporting options.

Program/Department: 11 programs suspended or eliminated under Indiana HEA 1001 mandate
Notes: Indiana Commission for Higher Education voted April 1 to act on 11 Indiana State programs. Named cuts include: Master of Music, MA Geography, MS Genetic Counseling, MA Industrial Technology. Part of statewide HEA 1001 compliance cutting 584 programs across 7 Indiana public universities. Students enrolled in suspended/eliminated programs may finish degrees; new admissions cease fall 2026; full elimination by fall 2027.

Program/Department: Senior leadership layoffs and executive restructuring to close $40M deficit
Notes: Three senior administrators laid off March 31: Jerry Tarrer (former interim president/CEO, at college since 2017), Laurent Pernot (VP of strategic partnerships, previously chief of staff for 8 years), Jeffrey Reuter (associate VP of budget, planning and analysis since 2019). CIO Kathie Koch also departed same month. Part of broader restructuring announced by President Shantay Bolton including hiring freeze for nonessential admin positions and further spending cuts. Since January 2025: 48 full-time faculty laid off (32 tenured); year prior: 70 staff cut. Total deficit: $40M. Bolton also simultaneously added new administrators: Emmanuel Lalande (SVP enrollment strategy), Adriel Hilton (chief of staff), Maryann Schaefer (AVP admissions), Aubrie Willaert (VP development), Jeffrey Bethke (interim CFO), Adam Weiss (VP legal affairs). Restructuring shifting oversight to five deans per May 2, 2026 follow-up article. Implementation continues through fiscal year ending August 31, 2026. No further faculty layoffs currently planned per Provost McBride, though not ruled out if enrollment declines.

Program/Department: More than a dozen faculty non-renewed amid financial constraints
Notes: Non-renewal letters sent by Provost Dr. Ryan Sandefer citing "current financial constraints" and institutional restructuring. Sources indicate more than a dozen faculty affected; college declined to confirm any personnel figures. College described cuts as "necessary budget adjustments." Letters stated non-renewals do not reflect negatively on performance. Catholic Benedictine private institution in Duluth, MN. Student sit-in protest reported following cuts including a popular philosophy professor.

Program/Department: 10 career and technical programs eliminated, including architecture
Notes: Board unanimously voted to eliminate 10 career and technical education (CTE) programs, including all architecture programs and one certificate each from several other academic areas. Reasons cited: low enrollment, non-transferable credits, low completion rates, and lack of industry demand. No full-time faculty negatively impacted; no adjuncts losing jobs as they typically teach across multiple programs. Budget pressures driven by statewide tuition freeze and declining property tax revenue from appraisal freeze. Chancellor LeBlanc described cuts as addressing "obsolete" programs amid a "new reality" for the college budget.

Program/Department: Keller Center's 9 staff laid off; departments cut budgets 5-10%
Notes: All 9 staff at Keller Center for Innovation in Engineering Education laid off. Tenured faculty salaries frozen; all other staff raises capped at 1%. All departments cut 5-10% of budgets. Most staff hiring frozen. Driven by revised endowment return projection (8% vs historical 10.2-12%), translating to ~$11.3B less in endowment value over 10 years and ~$500M less in annual payouts. Additional pressures: rising healthcare costs, federal research grant suspensions, new 8% endowment tax. Endowment funds 65% of operating budget ($36.4B total). President Eisgruber warned more cuts are coming. Graduate stipends and undergraduate financial aid commitments preserved.

Program/Department: Library director, the only credentialed librarian, laid off
Notes: Library Director Dan McClure (9-year tenure) laid off effective March 19 with no reason given — college's only credentialed librarian (MLS degree). College plans to hire a part-time replacement; no timeline given. Around the same time, Automotive Repair and Historic Preservation & Restoration programs also eliminated. ~800 students enrolled. Driven by budget shortfall as costs rise faster than incoming funds. McClure taught Library Research Skills (1-credit information literacy course each quarter) and managed interlibrary loans, Open Educational Resources compliance (Oregon law), vendor contracts, and consortium memberships (Oregon Community College Library Association, Chinook Library Network).

Program/Department: 70+ programs cut or consolidated, incl. all linguistics degrees
Notes: 70+ programs, minors and certificates cut or consolidated to address $45M deficit. Major cuts: all linguistics degrees phased out (dept merged with World Languages, Literatures and Cultures effective Sept. 1); BA in Latino and Latin American Studies eliminated; MA in Women's and Gender Studies cut. 25 undergraduate minors eliminated including women's and gender studies, LGBTQ studies, Mexican American studies, Africana studies, Asian studies, dance, geology, and special education. 40+ certificate programs cut (avg. fewer than 2 students/year). Driven by sharp decline in international enrollment and reduced state funding. Faculty buyouts offered to those with 15+ years service (deadline April 10). Linguistics dept chair said faculty were not consulted. Faculty and staff impact TBD. Enrolled students may complete degrees; no new admissions to affected programs. ~47,000 total enrollment.

Program/Department: 17 low-completion degree programs sunset under Ohio SB1
Notes: 17 programs sunset per Ohio Advance Higher Education Act (SB1) mandate requiring 5+ annual degree conferrals averaged over 3 years. Originally 36 programs fell below threshold; 16 approved to merge with similar programs, 3 received ODHE waivers, 17 sunset. Programs closed include BA in African American Studies, BA in French, BA in Chemistry, BA in Dance, BFA in Interdisciplinary Arts, BM in Music Therapy, BA in Mathematics, BA in Physics, BA in Geological Sciences, and several associate degrees. Most disciplines continue via minors, BS alternatives or related programs. 16 additional programs being merged/combined. Currently enrolled students may complete degrees as outlined. Incoming applicants to be notified of alternatives.

Program/Department: 14 classified positions eliminated across 3 campuses amid $1.8M structural deficit
Notes: [staff] Board approved 9 classified positions eliminated at Contra Costa College (CCC): academic scheduling specialist, instructional assistant counseling/matriculation, office assistant II fine/media arts, program assistant welcome center/outreach, program coordinator dramatic arts, dean of enrollment services (cut next year), learning disabilities specialist DSPS, wellness coordinator, plus additional vacant positions. 6 positions cut at Diablo Valley (2 grant-funded), 1 at Los Medanos (14 total across district). Undocumented students program coordinator position initially included then reversed after student/community pressure. 120 layoff notices issued via bumping process; 69 subsequently rescinded as of April 30. Structural deficit $1.8M current year, worsening in future years. District gave 8% merit raises to top administrators in 2025 — criticized by union. Contra Costa College serves more vulnerable population (San Pablo area) but received disproportionate cuts. Wellness coordinator loss also eliminates 3 student worker positions. Local 1 SEIU represents classified staff. Board failed first vote March 13, called emergency meeting March 15 to approve under deadline.

Program/Department: College closing permanently at end of fall 2026
Notes: Board of Trustees voted to permanently close the college at the end of Fall 2026. Announced by President Jennifer Chrisler on March 14, 2026. Driven by $20M+ in debt, $3.7M operating deficit (2025), chronic enrollment decline since 2019 (when college did not admit an incoming class), and NECHE accreditor sustainability requirement. Five-year sustainability plan (2019-2024) fell short: raised $55M of $60M goal but could not grow enrollment sufficiently. Two student pathways offered: Completion (Division III students finish at Hampshire through Dec 2026) and Transfer (to Five College Consortium partners and others). Founded 1965; known for independent liberal arts model. Board stated closure decision came only after exhausting all alternatives; nearly all trustees are alumni.

Program/Department: School of Public Health staff and lecturer layoffs amid FY2027 budget shortfall
Notes: School of Public Health conducting Reduction in Force (RIF) including mid-contract lecturer layoffs and staff cuts. Lecturer Lex Eisenberg received layoff notice March 13 mid-contract. ~50 students, faculty and staff demonstrated April 22 outside annual awards ceremony demanding halt to cuts and financial transparency. Compensation allocation cut from $39.3M (FY2025) to $37M (FY2026); FY2027 shortfall projected. Root causes: 65-student drop in international enrollment 2024-25 (accelerating due to Trump travel ban affecting 19 countries and visa scrutiny); declining indirect cost recovery from federal research disruptions; 2023 one-time $2M investment in faculty/staff pay (including 19 new tenure-track faculty) created unsustainable compensation baseline. School relies ~80% on tuition and indirect cost recovery. Dean Corliss stated school remains committed to "world-class education and research." Interim Associate Dean Kidwell confirmed compensation increases and layoffs are structurally separate decisions. Epidemiology PhD admissions also paused for 2025-26 cycle due to NIH grant terminations (separate prior action).

Program/Department: Spanish degree (eliminated) and Medical Laboratory Science degree (suspended)
Notes: UMaine announced it will end its Spanish degree program and suspend new admissions to the Medical Laboratory Science degree, citing an $18M structural deficit. The university is also cutting $5.6M in costs and laying off staff. A Budget Town Hall was held March 23, 2026.

Program/Department: 7 classified positions eliminated gutting College to Career and Student Success programs
Notes: [staff] Board voted March 10 to eliminate 7 classified positions: 2 from College to Career (C2C) program (Mary Schexnaydre, student success coach 15 years; Noah Morris, employment services advisor 13 years) and 5 from Student Success program. C2C program goes from coordinator + 2 specialists to coordinator only. 23 new students joining C2C fall 2026 who were promised services that no longer exist. Program was named most successful in California in 2018, placing students into 400+ jobs. Budget driven: combined Morris/Schexnaydre salaries ($124,139) replaced by upgraded coordinator role costing $205,429 — net loss of 2 specialists with no budget savings. Part of $10M deficit multi-year strategy including executive pay cuts, hiring freeze, furloughs. Driven by declining enrollment and state funding. SEIU Local 1021 involved. Staff said DOR contract compliance at risk without specialized disability expertise.

Program/Department: Dance program eliminated; two legacy programs cut; 52 staff laid off
Notes: [staff] Portland State declared a financial crisis amid a $35M deficit and declining enrollment (down ~25% since 2010). PSU eliminated dance programming (April 2026), cut two additional legacy programs, and laid off 52 faculty and staff (confirmed May 14, 2026 by OPB). The university is also evaluating cuts or consolidations across 19 academic departments.

Program/Department: Downtown Center campus closed after 47 years
Notes: Downtown Center at 88 Fourth St (Fourth and Mission) closing after spring 2026; no classes scheduled for fall 2026. Campus opened 1979; 47 years old. Enrollment of 152 full-time equivalent students — far below California state minimum of 1,000 required to receive $2.2M annual state funding. 900 part-time students also affected. Culinary, fashion, and language classes relocated to under-enrolled campuses including Chinatown/North Beach Center. No employee job losses. College owns 84,000 sq ft building; exploring partnerships with educational institutions, community orgs, and the city. Downtown location increasingly isolated near shuttered SF Centre mall; English learners also scattered by ICE enforcement fears. CCSF enrollment has fallen from ~22,000 full-time equivalent students a decade ago to ~9,000 currently.

Program/Department: Various Programs
Notes: NJCU announced the reduction of its academic portfolio by 37 percent, which involved sunsetting 48 undergraduate programs, 24 minors, 28 graduate programs, 10 certificate programs, and one doctoral program.

Program/Department: At least 16 faculty laid off, mostly humanities, under Ohio SB1
Notes: At least 16 faculty laid off, mostly in humanities, effective end of academic year (pay and benefits through August). Board of trustees approved cuts in early February 2026. Driven by Ohio Advance Higher Education Act (SB1) compliance — requires eliminating programs with fewer than 5 graduates/year over 3 years — and ongoing fiscal distress including a $26M student tuition/fee backlog. Ohio Dept. of Higher Education placed CSU on fiscal watch in 2024. Prior year cuts included 33 staff and 7 faculty. HBCU; secured $400K+ in emergency student aid via UNCF partnership in January 2026.

Program/Department: 9 minors and 7 concentrations eliminated, incl. Economics and Cybersecurity
Notes: Board unanimously voted to eliminate 9 minors and 7 concentrations (16 total), saving ~$400K. Minors cut include African American Studies, Cybersecurity, Economics, Latin American Studies, Management Information Systems, Non-profit Studies, Peace and Justice Studies, Philosophy and Religion, and Professional Writing. Current students with declared minors/concentrations may finish via teach-out. Second round of cuts after 6 programs were eliminated in May 2025. Part of effort to close ~$8M shortfall. Combined with fee increases, generates ~$800K. 4 athletic teams (men's/women's swimming and tennis) also recommended for elimination but decision deferred to May 2026 board meeting. Tuition increase not pursued for 2026-27.

Program/Department: College ceasing operations Aug. 31, 2026; nursing moves to Curry College
Notes: Labouré College of Healthcare (founded 1892, 134 years) will cease all academic operations August 31, 2026. Board of Directors unanimously approved merger/acquisition agreement with Curry College (~4 miles away in Milton, MA). Nursing programs will transfer to Curry's School of Nursing and Health Sciences under a new unit called the Labouré Center for Advancing Healthcare Opportunity. Reasons cited: persistent financial and enrollment challenges, and regulatory hurdles (state regulators voted to shut down nursing program in 2023 after students failed 80% first-time NCLEX pass rate threshold; decision overturned on appeal; scores restored to full approval by May 2024). Enrollment declined from peak of 1,188 (fall 2020) to 530 (fall 2024), roughly a 55% drop. Only 168 new students enrolled in 2025 vs. goal of 300. ASN nursing students (majority of enrollment) will transfer to Curry's Milton campus in fall 2026; tuition and fees held at 2026-2027 Labouré rates; credits transfer seamlessly. Students in other programs (e.g. respiratory care) being directed to articulation agreements at other institutions if unable to complete by Aug. 31. Curry plans to hire ~15 Labouré nursing faculty and ~20 staff (35-40 total of ~100 total Labouré employees). As of Nov. 1, 2024: 23 FT instructional employees, 49 noninstructional staff at Labouré. Labouré endowment pledged to support the new Center. Labouré plans to sell its physical property (303 Adams St, Milton — former Aquinas College campus) and use proceeds to fund the Center. Curry enrolled ~2,000 students in fall 2024 and also faced enrollment declines; acquisition expected to potentially double Curry nursing enrollment. Deal subject to regulatory approval at time of announcement.

Program/Department: Adaptive PE program discontinued; 16 staff laid off, 17 vacancies cut
Notes: Board voted 4-2 to lay off 16 non-faculty workers and eliminate 17 vacant positions (33 total). Adaptive Physical Education (APE) program discontinued beginning 2026-27; offered for 40+ years serving ~200 disabled students. Cuts also include 3 Disability Support Programs roles. Driven by loss of HSI federal grants, stagnating state funding, and local property tax underperformance. Projected deficit of $3.75M in 2027 and $4.4M in 2028 without action. Board declared financial hardship via resolution.

Program/Department: Permanent institution closure after 68 years
Notes: [staff] 387 total employees losing jobs via WARN filing: 26 assistant professors, 106 adjuncts, 14 head coaches, ~31 federal work-study students, ~49 student employees, and remaining admin/staff. Terminations begin May 15 through Sept. 30, 2026. Founded 1958 by Sisters of St. Francis of Sylvania; owned and subsidized by Sisters for nearly 25 years. Closure driven by declining enrollment, rising costs, and unsustainable funding model. President William Bisset stepped down; Sister Nancy Linenkugel named 13th and final president. Teach-out agreements with University of Toledo (dedicated transfer process), Walsh University, Trine University, and Marietta College. ~1,200 students affected. No bumping rights or union representation for laid-off staff.

Program/Department: 60 staff layoffs and 10 vacant positions eliminated to address $17.5M structural deficit
Notes: [staff] Board voted February 9 to lay off ~60 classified staff and eliminate equivalent of ~10 vacant positions. All 49 classified management and 46 academic administrator positions also opened to potential elimination in coming weeks restructuring. Structural deficit projected to reach $17.5M in FY2027 nearly wiping out reserves. College scraped together $6.3M in one-off funds reducing current deficit to $5.8M. Trustee blowback during Feb 9 meeting. Part of broader California community college funding crisis.

Program/Department: Environmental Geography BS, 2 master's, 2 minors and 3 certificates deactivated
Notes: Deactivating 1 undergraduate program (Environmental Geography, B.S.), 2 graduate programs (Conflict Analysis and Resolution, M.S.; Higher Education and Student Affairs Administration, M.S.), 2 minors, and 3 certificates. 19 students in impacted bachelor's programs, 29 in master's programs (48 total; 0.8% of enrollment). Enrolled students may complete degrees via teach-out. Part of SUNY-mandated Framework for Fiscal Stability Plan targeting elimination of $16-17M structural deficit by 2027-28. Deficit attributed to Great Recession-era state cuts and COVID-19 financial losses. Prior year cuts included sociology. Faculty union UUP held campus rally March 10 demanding state funding.

Program/Department: Permanent institution closure after 20 years of operation
Notes: Board of Trustees voted February 7, 2026 to cease academic operations at end of 2025-2026 academic year. Founded 2002, incorporated in CA; first class admitted 2005; Reformed Christian liberal arts institution in Old Town Pasadena. Closure driven by declining enrollment, rising operational costs (Southern California), heightened accreditation expectations, and loss of federal funds. Accreditation held by WASC Senior (on probation at time of closure). Over half of full-time students scheduled to graduate May 2026; teach-out agreements established with local Christian colleges and sister institutions for underclassmen. Staff and faculty given advance notice to find next positions. Board explored decreased operational expenses, additional student recruitment, and campus relocation before concluding closure was only remaining option. Source is the official college closure announcement page.

Program/Department: 22 staff laid off in administrative reorganization
Notes: 22 staff laid off (18 full-time, 4 part-time) via reorganizations, staffing consolidations and reductions across administrative offices. Majority are non-student-facing roles. No faculty affected. Enrollment has dropped from 2,033 in 2011-12 to 1,600+ currently. Driven by declining birth rates, fewer students choosing college, and reduced international enrollment. Endowment remains strong at ~$370M. Board of Trustees approved to return college to balanced budget.

Program/Department: College of Education dissolved; 45 positions eliminated
Notes: 45 total positions eliminated (12 faculty, 21 staff, 11 administrators; ~40% currently vacant). College of Education (est. 1958) dissolved and absorbed into new College of Humanities, Education and Social Science (CHESS), saving ~$1.8M. Biology dept split: biochemistry, microbiology, and anatomy & physiology merged with pharmacy's pharmaceutical sciences into new Dept of Biomedical Sciences under Kasiska Division of Health Sciences. Driven by $8M deficit from 3% state-mandated budget cut plus $3M health insurance increases and $2.2M in unfunded cost adjustments. Accreditation concerns raised by former College of Education dean.

Program/Department: About 40 dining staff positions eliminated; early retirement offered
Notes: All ~40 college-employed dining staff positions eliminated after spring 2026 semester; staff may apply to continue with dining contractor Bon Appétit. Early retirement incentive offered to all employees 60+ with 10+ years of service (2 weeks pay per year worked, up to 18 months). Driven by missed enrollment goals for 2 consecutive years. No faculty positions affected. Tuition benefit preserved for early retirees with currently enrolled dependents.

Program/Department: Staff layoff
Notes: SMC eliminating ~70 classified and management positions in response to $16.7M projected deficit that could deplete financial reserves by 2026-27, after already implementing $8.6M in prior budget reductions. Declining enrollment drives the shortfall. Cuts target classified staff and management; no faculty layoffs announced at this stage.

Program/Department: Women's and Gender Studies program ended to comply with system policies
Notes: Women's and Gender Studies (WGST) program closed effective immediately per Interim President Tommy Williams. Impacts BA/BS degrees, undergraduate minor, and graduate certificate. 25 enrolled majors and 31 enrolled minors (56 total) will be taught out over up to 6 semesters. 50+ affiliated faculty employment status unaffected. Cited Texas A&M System policy compliance and limited enrollment. Part of broader spring 2026 course review covering ~5,400 syllabi; 6 courses also canceled for non-compliance.

Program/Department: 5 Athletics staff positions eliminated
Notes: [staff] WSU Athletics eliminated five staff positions in late January 2026 to "structure and right-size" its operations. Cuts driven by financial pressures from the House vs. NCAA settlement, which requires universities to directly compensate student-athletes. AD Kevin Saal had requested $1M in NIL donations in April 2025 to support men's basketball. Cuts coincided with KU and K-State also seeking government assistance for athletic funding. Broader context: WSU also announced a 7% general use budget cut ($7.9M reduction for next fiscal year), and the College of Engineering had eliminated at least seven employees in December 2025. WSU had record enrollment but noted headcount alone does not translate to revenue growth.

Program/Department: Admissions paused for 5 Ph.D. programs for fall 2026
Notes: Admissions paused for fall 2026 in 5 Ph.D. programs: Clinical Psychology, Anthropology, Human Paleobiology, Political Science, and Mathematics. Applicants notified week of Jan 19; application fees refunded; offered consideration for master's programs instead. University cited need to limit new funding commitments to protect existing Ph.D. student packages. Not described as permanent closure. Separately, total Ph.D. packages across all Columbian College of Arts & Sciences departments also slashed (GWU declined to confirm details). Clinical Psych admitted record-low 3 students fall 2025 (typical: 8-9); APA cohort size requirements led to zero admits rather than partial cohort. Math had zero remaining funding after covering continuing students. Human Paleobiology admits ~3/year; timing tied to current student graduation. International enrollment down ~13% of total fall 2025; Trump-era visa/travel changes cited. President Granberg ordered all schools to prepare FY2027 budget contingency plans.

Program/Department: 4 student support centers closed and 23 Academic Affairs positions eliminated
Notes: [staff] Provost William Inboden announced January 17 closure of 4 student support centers effective end of spring 2026: Center for Teaching and Learning (longstanding faculty instructional support); Office of Community Engagement (community partnerships, previously Division of Diversity and Community Engagement under SB 17); Vick Advising Excellence Center (core curriculum/major-switching advising); Office of Undergraduate Research (interdisciplinary research connections for undergrads). 23 Academic Affairs staff positions eliminated — 3 of 8 office leaders including head of interdisciplinary studies. Layoffs described as sudden with no prior warning. Resources "repurposed" across colleges per provost; faculty and students skeptical adequate alternatives exist. Separate April 2024 action: 49+ employees laid off and Division of Campus and Community Engagement disbanded under SB 17 compliance. Separate February 2026 action: UT Austin closing American Studies department, consolidating gender/ethnic studies and language departments into new "Department of Social and Cultural Analysis" — distinct action not driven by budget. UT System-wide budget pressure from state appropriations; no endowment draw needed. Inboden fired prior Academic Affairs head Art Markman over "ideological differences" fall 2025.

Program/Department: Adaptive Athletics Program (Wheelchair Basketball) Discontinued
Notes: Eastern Washington University announced the discontinuation of its Division I adaptive athletics program (wheelchair basketball) at the end of the 2025-26 academic season due to sustainability and financial challenges. The program was the first of its kind in the Pacific Northwest.

Program/Department: College closing after 2026-27; Vanderbilt acquiring campus
Notes: California College of the Arts closing permanently end of 2026-27 academic year after 119 years. Founded 1907 in East Bay; moved to SF Design District campus ($123M building opened 2025). Vanderbilt University acquiring SF campus and original Oakland property; will establish own undergraduate and graduate programming. CCA Institute and Wattis Institute of Contemporary Arts museum preserved at campus. No current CCA faculty guaranteed jobs under Vanderbilt. 28 non-faculty staff positions eliminated end of spring 2026 semester (mostly union workers). Driven by $20M structural deficit, years of enrollment decline, and tuition-dependent model unsustainable at ~$100M operating budget. Despite $22.5M in private donations in 2025 (matched by Nvidia CEO Jen-Hsun Huang Foundation) and $20M gift — all stop-gap measures. Students graduating by end of 2026-27 receive CCA degrees; others must transfer. No new students admitted fall 2027. Closes same year as prior Bay Area art school wave: SFAI (2022), Mills College merger with Northeastern (2022). Mayor Daniel Lurie attended press conference alongside Vanderbilt Chancellor Diermeier. Last standalone art and design college in San Francisco.

Program/Department: NCAA Division I women's equestrian program eliminated — replaced by STUNT varsity program
Notes: Athletic Director Rocko DeLuca announced January 9 elimination of NCAA Division I women's equestrian team effective end of 2025-26 season — team had just won its third conference championship (undefeated season). 33 student-athletes affected. Program transitioned to club sport; STUNT simultaneously elevated from club to NCAA varsity status. Decision made primarily on budget grounds citing $1M+ annual savings. Three active lawsuits alleging fraud and misrepresentation: parents' suit (filed Feb 9), wire fraud investigation by UC Davis police department (AD DeLuca continued soliciting donations after decision was made internally), Title IX concerns (program elevated to D1 as part of Title IX settlement, then eliminated despite championship success while men's programs retained). Independent audit commissioned by parents found original cost report over-estimated expenses by 120%+ ($850K+) — alleged budget inflation through misrepresenting operating expenses, removing legitimate revenue, counting fictional offset as real expense. Metadata on consultant report shows it was completed after the decision was made — used to justify not inform. UC Davis chancellor ordered 10% budget cuts February 2025; equestrian placed on chopping block March 2025 internally; public announcement January 2026 after months of continued recruiting and donation solicitation. UC Davis reviewing its own financial records; findings due June 30 (team's final day). 30 horses donated to program by community members face uncertain future. Parents offered privately funded endowment to sustain program — university rejected offer.

Program/Department: Football Program Suspended
Notes: Program suspended after multiple seasons of losses, financial unsustainability, and media investigations. Head coach Desmond Gumbs stepped down; intent to return in Division II.

Program/Department: Staff Layoffs
Notes: Restructuring to address structural budget imbalances, cutting 33 positions and redesigning 30 others as part of $4 million realignment.

Program/Department: 109 positions eliminated including 45 teaching faculty amid $18M budget cuts
Notes: 109 total positions reduced: 47 eliminated/non-renewed Dec 18 (25 teaching faculty incl. 5 tenured, 22 admin faculty), plus 31 from hiring freeze since May 2025, 22 voluntary separations/incentivized retirements, 9 recent retirements. 45 teaching faculty + 64 admin faculty/staff total. Non-tenured staff/admin conclude June 30, 2026; tenured faculty conclude June 30, 2027 (or early retirement option). Earlham was Wayne County's 7th-largest employer (388 total employees pre-cuts). Enrollment dropped from ~1,200 students (2007) to 671 fall 2025. Structural cash-flow deficit of ~$15M/year for nearly a decade; board mandated balanced budget by 2030 requiring $18M in recurring expense cuts. Specific academic programs/majors to be reduced or discontinued TBD by faculty committees spring 2026. Quaker-affiliated liberal arts institution founded 1847. Follow-up April 2026: some majors confirmed ended per March 30 president email.

Program/Department: Staff layoff
Notes: 16 full-time faculty members issued non-renewal notices effective end of spring 2026 semester as university targets a 12:1 student-faculty ratio. Layoffs follow the lifting of financial probation by the Southern Association of Colleges and Schools (SACSCOC). Affected faculty represent multiple academic departments at the Memphis institution.

Institution: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
Program/Department: 6 international area studies centers closed and 8 other centers/institutes eliminated — $7M savings target
Notes: [staff] All 6 area studies research centers permanently closed following loss of Title VI federal funding: Center for European Studies, African Studies Center, Carolina Asia Center, Center for Middle East and Islamic Studies, Institute for the Study of the Americas, Center for Slavic/Eurasian/East European Studies. 8 additional centers and institutes also closed (14 of 59 total). Saves $4.8M of $7M centers/institutes target; $3M in near-term savings. Broader $70M+ budget reduction plan announced July 2025 by Chancellor Lee Roberts targets $25M in administrative spending. Jan 2026: Board of Trustees surprise resolution added $16.5M in additional cuts (5% of administrative salary base). Area studies closures driven by UNC CFO Nate Knuffman recommendation; Dean White and Senior Associate Dean McDonald cited Title VI funding loss as precipitating factor. Faculty Council passed resolution opposing closures. Multiple faculty and student petitions filed. Part of $85M+ total cuts plan across federal research reductions (100 fewer HHS grants), state funding uncertainty, and administrative efficiency initiatives. Faculty strongly opposed; UE150 graduate workers union commissioned independent financial audit finding cuts not necessary given UNC's financial position. Separate: $2M targeted at "low-performing" academic programs (decisions pending). UNC-CH operates on $4.79B all-funds budget.

Program/Department: Staff layoff
Notes: 114 staff members laid off effective December 12, 2025, representing 7.6% of 1,493 full-time and part-time employees. Cuts announced jointly by President Robert L. Manuel, Provost Salma Ghanem, and CFO. DePaul has faced declining enrollment and rising costs for several years; layoffs framed as necessary for structural financial sustainability.

Institution: Lake Forest Graduate School of Management
Program/Department: MBA program and institution permanently closing after 80 years
Notes: [staff] Ceasing all MBA academic operations and closing as an accredited institution June 30, 2026. Founded 1946 to serve WWII veterans; 80 years of operation. Enrollment dropped ~50% between 2020 and 2024 (393 graduate students at peak, ~196 at closure). President and CEO Carrie Buchwald cited declining enrollment making program "unsustainable" after considering multiple strategic options. Current students offered seamless transfer to Excelsior University (nonprofit, Albany NY; Middle States accredited) to complete MBA online. Eligible students may apply for Closed School Loan Discharge. Institution continues non-academic operations via Lake Forest Center for Leadership (leadership development consulting). Announced via LinkedIn post and letter to students and faculty December 13-14, 2025.
